It combines the exact Dirichlet calibration theorem of Vlassis and Thomas [Vlassis and Thomas, 2026], which resolves Gaffke's conjecture in statistics, with results in convex geometry including Grünbaum's centroid theorem [Grünbaum, 1960] and its generalization by Letwin and Yaskin [Letwin and Yaskin, 2024].

input: I identify and challenge several deeply ingrained methodological habits that together produce systematic failures in the statistical analysis of clinical research. These problematic practices include: (1) an excessive reliance on hypothesis testing as the main method for comparing treatments, (2) a disconnect between the statistical techniques used to assess predictive accuracy and the conditions of real clinical practice, (3) the flawed use of meta-analytic methods when pooling results across multiple studies, and (4) a pervasive inclination toward overconfident research conclusions. Three interconnected forces seem to sustain this dysfunctional status quo: (i) inadequate statistical training in medical school and residency programs, (ii) the disproportionate power that biostatistical consultants hold over funding decisions and publication outcomes, and (iii) the standards and expectations set by funding agencies, academic journals, and regulatory bodies. I contend that substantive reform across these educational and institutional structures is essential to break the present cycle and elevate the standard of statistical practice in clinical research.
target: I critique a set of entrenched methodological conventions that collectively create systemic dysfunction in statistical research for clinical decisions. These include: (1) the prevalent use of hypothesis tests to compare treatments, (2) remoteness from patient care of the methods used to evaluate the accuracy of predictions of patient outcomes, (3) poor practice of meta-analysis to combine findings across studies, and (4) widespread research with incredible certitude. It appears that the dysfunction is held in place by three factors: (i) rudimentary instruction in statistical methodology received by medical students and residents, (ii) reliance of clinical researchers on consulting biostatisticians, wo act as statistical gatekeepers in evaluation of grant proposals and paper submissions, and (iii) institutional practices of research funding agencies, medical journals, and governmental bodies that regulate medical treatment. I conjecture that systemic changes are necessary to break the existing impasse, moving statistical research to a better equilibrium.

input:
Perturbative-NeuSA addresses a core limitation of neural spectral PDE solvers: such methods generally learn an entire unresolved vector field, even in cases where an inexpensive, simple approximate model can already reproduce most of the solution trajectory. We propose a residual framework that splits the target solution into two components—a low-fidelity background model and a high-resolution perturbation—allowing the neural network to focus exclusively on learning the unresolved dynamics.

Built from the exact perturbation equation, our method integrates four elements: a fixed spectral operator, a correction term that depends on the background solution, the background defect intrinsic to the target PDE, and an optional neural closure term. This design makes it possible to evaluate the roles of physical structure and neural learning separately.

Experiments on 2D Burgers, Klein-Gordon, and heterogeneous 2D wave equations demonstrate that the deterministic structured solver surpasses the trained baseline without any neural training at all. The largest improvements appear in Burgers, where deterministic corrections cut training and extrapolation errors by factors of 24 and 44, respectively. For Klein-Gordon, varying background resolution across seven levels reveals that neural closure operates selectively: it enhances weak backgrounds (3.6× gain), has minimal effect at intermediate resolutions, and worsens accurate backgrounds. The wave equation, in contrast, gains an additional 18% error reduction when the remaining residuals are concentrated near interfaces.

Analysis across several initial conditions indicates that closure effectiveness hinges on the spectral properties of the initial condition and can vanish during extrapolation once structured correction already captures the dominant dynamics.

Perturbative-NeuSA therefore recasts neural closure as a selective, measurable refinement determined by background quality, residual structure, and alignment with the closure approach.
target: Neural spectral PDE solvers often learn an entire unresolved vector field even when an inexpensive approximate model can already capture most of the trajectory. Here we introduce Perturbative-NeuSA, a residual formulation that decomposes the target solution into a low-fidelity background and a high-resolution perturbation, so that only the unresolved dynamics is learned. Starting from the exact perturbation equation, the method combines a fixed spectral operator, a background-dependent correction, the background defect in the target PDE, and an optional neural closure. This construction makes the roles of physical structure and neural closure separately measurable. Across 2D Burgers, Klein-Gordon, and heterogeneous 2D wave equations, the deterministic structured solver outperforms the trained NeuSA baseline while requiring no neural-network training. The largest gains occur on Burgers, where the deterministic correction reduces training and extrapolation errors by factors of 24 and 44, respectively. In addition, a Klein-Gordon sweep over seven background resolutions shows that the effect of the closure is conditional: it improves a poor background by 3.6 times, becomes neutral at intermediate resolutions, and degrades a well-resolved background. For the wave equation, however, the closure provides an additional 18% reduction when the remaining residual is interface-localized. Multi-initial-condition diagnostics further show that the useful closure regime depends on the initial-condition spectrum and can disappear in extrapolation when structured correction already captures the dominant Burgers dynamics. Perturbative-NeuSA therefore reframes neural closure as a conditional, diagnosable correction governed by background fidelity, residual organization, and compatibility with the closure model.

input:
Majority dynamics describes a two-opinion process where every vertex repeatedly takes on whichever opinion is held by most of its neighbors. We examine this process on a resampled sparse binary stochastic block model within the assortative regime. At each step, a fresh graph is sampled from the distribution defined by the current partition of opinions: two vertices with the same opinion become connected with probability $\alpha = a\log N/N$, whereas two vertices with differing opinions become connected with probability $\beta = b\log N/N$, where $a > b > 1$. Let $B_t$ and $R_t$ represent the sizes of the blue and red camps at time $t$. We demonstrate that the weighted advantage $\widetilde{\Delta}_t = b|B_t| - a|R_t|$—rather than the unweighted advantage $\Delta_t = |B_t| - |R_t|$ by itself—controls how quickly unanimity is attained. Our results, valid with high probability as $N \to \infty$, split the blue unanimity problem (under the assumption of an initial blue advantage $\Delta_0 > 0$) into three temporal regimes: constant, subpolynomial, and polynomial time.

First, if $\widetilde{\Delta}_0 \gtrsim -N/\sqrt{\log N}$, blue unanimity is reached within three updates. Second, if $\widetilde{\Delta}_0 < 0$ and $|\widetilde{\Delta}_0| = o(N)$, blue unanimity is reached within $N^{o(1)}$ updates. Moreover, when $\widetilde{\Delta}_0 < 0$, $|\widetilde{\Delta}_0| = O(N)$, and $\Delta_0 \gg \sqrt{N/\log N}$, blue unanimity is nonetheless reached within $N^{I_0 + o(1)}$ updates, where
$$I_0 = \left(\mathbf{ReLU}\!\Big(\sqrt{a\,\tfrac{|R_0|}{N}} - \sqrt{b\,\tfrac{|B_0|}{N}}\Big)\right)^2.$$
Conversely, outside the weighted threshold region, if $|B_0|/|R_0| \leq a/b - \kappa$ and $\Delta_0 > 0$, then at least $N^{I_0 - o(1)}$ updates are required for blue unanimity. The proofs depend on sharp bounds for single-vertex flip probabilities in sparse binomial differences, a technique that may find applications beyond the current context.
target: Majority dynamics is a two-opinion process in which each vertex repeatedly updates to the majority opinion among its neighbors. We study this process on a resampled sparse binary stochastic block model in the assortative regime. At each time step, a graph is sampled from the current opinion partition: vertices with the same opinion are joined with probability $α=a\log N/N$, while vertices with differing opinions are joined with probability $β=b\log N/N$, where $a>b>1$. Let $B_t$ and $R_t$ denote the blue and red camps at time $t$. We show that the weighted advantage $\widetildeΔ_t =b|B_t|-a|R_t|$, rather than the unweighted advantage $Δ_t=|B_t|-|R_t|$ alone, governs the pace to unanimity. Our results, which hold with high probability as \(N\to\infty\), identify three regimes for blue unanimity under the initial blue advantage, i.e., $Δ_0>0$: constant time, subpolynomial time, and polynomial time. First, when $\widetildeΔ_0 \gtrsim -N/\sqrt{\log N}$, blue unanimity occurs within three updates. Second, when $\widetildeΔ_0 < 0$ and $|\widetildeΔ_0| = o(N)$, blue unanimity occurs within $N^{o(1)}$ updates. Furthermore, when $\widetildeΔ_0 < 0$, $|\widetildeΔ_0| = O(N)$, and $Δ_0\gg\sqrt{N/\log N}$, blue unanimity still occurs within $N^{I_0+o(1)}$ updates, where \[ I_0= \left(\mathbf{ReLU}\Big(\sqrt{a\frac{|R_0|}{N}}-\sqrt{b\frac{|B_0|}{N}}\Big)\right)^2, \] and $\mathbf{ReLU}(x)=\max\{x,0\}$. Conversely, away from the weighted threshold, when $|B_0|/|R_0|\le a/b-κ$ and $Δ_0>0$, $N^{I_0 - o(1)}$ updates are necessary for blue unanimity. Our analysis relies on detailed estimates for one-vertex flip probabilities in sparse binomial differences, which could be of independent interest.

input: We investigate how quickly the Euler-Maruyama scheme converges in the strong sense when applied to additive stochastic differential equations with fractional Brownian motion noise (Hurst parameter $H \in (0,1)$). Under the assumption that the drift coefficient satisfies a Lipschitz condition, we establish convergence rates of $1$ for $H \in (1/2,1)$ and $1/2+H-\varepsilon$ (for arbitrarily small $\varepsilon>0$) for $H \in (0,1/2]$. The proof relies crucially on a displaced sewing technique in the stochastic setting, which leverages the conditional Gaussian nature of fractional Brownian motion to bound errors arising from temporal discretization of the noise.
target: We study the strong convergence rate of the Euler-Maruyama scheme for additive stochastic differential equations driven by a fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter $H \in (0,1)$. Assuming the drift coefficient to be Lipschitz continuous, we show that the rate is $1$ if $H \in (1/2,1)$, and $1/2+H-\varepsilon$, for any $\varepsilon>0$, if $H \in (0,1/2]$. The main ingredient is a shifted stochastic sewing argument, which exploits the conditional Gaussian structure of fractional Brownian motion to control the noise discretization error.

input: A well-established finding in high-dimensional statistical theory is that a constant aspect ratio—defined by the limit $n/d\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$ as both the sample size $n$ and dimension $d$ grow without bound—plays a central role in describing the fundamental performance limits of standard estimation problems. A representative example is the estimation of the leading eigenvector of a $d\times d$ population covariance matrix from $n$ independent samples: the BBP phase transition pinpoints an exact threshold, expressible as a simple function of the aspect ratio, below which the top sample principal component has zero asymptotic correlation with the true eigenvector, and above which this correlation becomes strictly positive. The present work shows, however, that online (streaming) algorithms behave in a fundamentally different manner, and that a constant aspect ratio is insufficient to achieve nonzero overlap. We study Oja's algorithm, the canonical method for online PCA. Specifically, for the model $\Sigma=\theta^2 v_0v_0^\top+I\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$, with Oja's algorithm run at step size $\delta/d$ on $n$ iid samples $X_k\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)$ to produce the estimate $\hat{v}_n$, we establish a phase transition in the regime $n,d\to\infty$ with $n/d\log d\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$. The correlation $|\langle\hat{v}_n,v_0\rangle|$ vanishes when $\gamma<\gamma_*$ and converges to $\rho_*$ when $\gamma>\gamma_*$. The critical threshold and limiting correlation are given explicitly by $\rho_*=\rho_*(\theta,\delta)=\sqrt{(\theta^2-\delta/2)_+/\theta^2(1+\delta/2)}$ and $\gamma_*=\gamma_*(\theta,\delta)=1/2\delta(\theta^2-\delta/2)_+$. Precisely at the critical point, when $n=\lfloor\gamma_* d\log d+\eta d\rfloor$ as $d\to\infty$ for fixed $\eta\in\mathbb{R}$, the correlation is itself random: $|\langle\hat{v}_n,v_0\rangle|\stackrel{w}{\to}\rho_*|G|\exp(\eta/2\gamma_*)/\sqrt{\rho_*^4+G^2\exp(\eta/\gamma_*)}$ where $G\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$. This stands in sharp contrast to standard high-dimensional PCA, in which a constant sample-to-dimension ratio already suffices for nonzero overlap, which then increases monotonically as $n/d$ grows.
target: High dimensional statistical theory has established the importance of constant aspect ratio, when the number of dimensions ($d$) and samples ($n$) satisfy $n,d\to\infty$ with $n/d\to γ\in(0,\infty)$, in understanding the limits of canonical estimation problems. In particular, for estimating the top eigenvector of a $d\times d$ population covariance matrix from $n$ iid samples, the BBP phase transition gives a precise threshold -- a simple functional of the aspect ratio -- such that the top sample principal component attains nonzero asymptotic correlation with the truth only when the leading population eigenvalue exceeds it. In this paper, we show that for online / streaming algorithms the story is very different, and constant aspect ratio is insufficient for nonzero overlap. We study Oja's algorithm, the most popular method for online PCA. Let $Σ=θ^2 v_0v_0^\top+I\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$, and run Oja's algorithm with step size $δ/d$ on $n$ iid samples $X_k\sim\mathcal{N}(0,Σ)$, with output $\hat v_n$. Then, as $n,d\to\infty$ with $n/d\log d\toγ\in(0,\infty)$, we establish a phase transition: $|\langle\hat v_n,v_0\rangle|\to 0$ when $γ<γ_*$, and $\toρ_*$ when $γ>γ_*$. Here $ρ_*=ρ_*(θ,δ)=\sqrt{(θ^2-δ/2)_+/θ^2(1+δ/2)}$ and $γ_*=γ_*(θ,δ)=1/2δ(θ^2-δ/2)_+$. Further, at criticality, when $n=[γ_*d\log d+ηd]$ and $d\to\infty$, $η\in\mathbb{R}$, the correlation is random: $|\langle\hat v_n,v_0\rangle|\stackrel{w}{\to}ρ_*|G|\exp(η/2γ_*)/\sqrt{ρ_*^4+G^2\exp(η/γ_*)}$ where $G\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$. This is in stark contrast to ordinary high dimensional PCA, where nonzero overlap is possible at constant $n/d$ and improves as $n/d$ increases.

input: New research has shown that many animal species employ a two-nostril 'stereo' sense of smell. This paper offers initial theoretical calculations that explore the circumstances under which stereo olfaction confers benefits compared to single-nostril 'mono' olfaction. Our results suggest that stereo olfaction is advantageous when odour concentration displays significant relative variation and when air correlations extend over large spatial scales, especially within boundary layers near surfaces. Stereo olfaction is therefore most useful when animals are locating olfactory boundaries on surfaces—such as when following scent trails.
target: Recent works have highlighted the use of dual nostril 'stereo' olfaction by a variety of animals. In this work we perform "back of the envelope" calculations to determine when stereo olfaction is useful compared to single nostril 'mono' olfaction. We find that stereo olfaction is advantageous when there are large relative changes in the odour concentration, and when the spatial length scales of correlations in air are large, such as in the boundary layer near surfaces. In other words, stereo olfaction is useful when animals are searching surfaces for olfactory edges, such as when tracking odour trails.

Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) hold considerable promise for reshaping clinical practice. Yet deploying them effectively in medical environments demands solving a core vision-related challenge: these models must learn from a wide variety of 2D and 3D medical images, and their evaluation must mirror the way radiologists operate clinically while producing precise, detailed, and accurate outputs.

This paper introduces ClinFusion, a vision-centric MLLM designed to deliver comprehensive medical analysis by methodically addressing these challenges. Its primary contributions include a hierarchical vision encoder architecture featuring a Cascade Spatial-Aware Locality Fusion operator that unifies both conventional 2D and native 3D medical image analysis within a single encoder. We also propose a vision-oriented evaluation framework consisting of MedIF-Bench for assessing instruction-following ability and a region-of-interest-grounded methodology for clinically relevant, accuracy-focused report evaluation.

ClinFusion achieves state-of-the-art results across broad 2D and 3D multimodal medical evaluation suites—spanning visual question answering, report generation, and instruction following—as well as purely text-based medical tasks. It outperforms leading open-source medical MLLMs, including Hulu-Med and Lingshu, on 20 of 24 benchmarks and surpasses proprietary models such as GPT-5.2 and Gemini-3-Flash on 13 of 16 benchmarks. The framework can further be augmented with agent-based tools to support retrieval-augmented and tool-assisted clinical workflows. Independent evaluation by board-certified radiologists confirms that ClinFusion produces higher-quality reports and validates our region-of-interest-grounded evaluation metric as the most closely aligned with expert judgment among all automated metrics tested.
target: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) hold immense potential to revolutionize clinical practice, yet deploying them in the medical domain is fundamentally a vision-centric challenge: models must absorb knowledge from heterogeneous 2D and 3D medical images, and evaluation protocols must align with radiologists' clinical practice and provide an accurate, fine-grained and factualness-driven assessment. In this paper, we introduce ClinFusion, a vision-centric MLLM designed for holistic medical understanding that systematically addresses these limitations. We propose a compositional and cascaded vision encoder architecture featuring a Cascade Spatial-Aware Locality Fusion operator that unifies diverse 2D and native 3D medical image understanding within a fused encoder. We further introduce a vision-grounded evaluation framework, including MedIF-Bench for instruction-following assessment and a region-of-interest-grounded method for clinically aligned and factualness-driven report generation evaluation. We show that ClinFusion sets a new state-of-the-art across a comprehensive suite of 2D and 3D multimodal medical benchmarks---spanning visual question answering, report generation, and instruction following---as well as textual medical tasks, outperforming leading open-source medical MLLMs (\textit{e.g.}, Hulu-Med, Lingshu) on 20 out of 24 benchmarks and demonstrating multimodal capabilities better than powerful proprietary models such as GPT-5.2 and Gemini-3-Flash on 13 out of 16 benchmarks, and can be further augmented with agentic tool use for retrieval-augmented and tool-assisted clinical workflows. A blinded evaluation by board-certified radiologists confirms that ClinFusion produces the highest-ranked reports, and validates our RoI-grounded metric as achieving the strongest correlation with expert judgment among all automatic evaluation metrics examined.

input: This research investigates memorization patterns in discriminatively trained reward models (RMs) by analyzing counterfactual memorization across two datasets of human preferences. The study demonstrates that RMs exhibit three key limitations: 1) they concentrate memorization efforts on straightforward preference pairs with large margins, 2) they retain dataset-particular patterns (such as specific model characteristics and user selection methods), and 3) they apply oversimplified heuristic associations with human preference (including factors like response length and rule adherence) when encountering novel preference pairs. Collectively, these results suggest that using discriminative training to develop RMs from human preference data produces biased models that lack the sophistication required to accurately evaluate response quality when preferences vary by context.
target: This paper studies what discriminatively trained reward models (RMs) memorize by measuring counterfactual memorization on two human preference datasets. We show that RMs 1) misallocate memorization to easy, high margin preference pairs, 2) memorize dataset-specific shortcuts (e.g., model identity, user sampling strategy), and 3) overgeneralize simple heuristic correlates of human preference (e.g., length, compliance) when confronted with unseen preference pairs. Overall, our findings indicate that discriminative training of RMs from human preference data results in biased RMs not yet capable of judging response quality in context-dependent scenarios.

The myth of Hermes and Argus Panoptes tells of a giant with innumerable eyes who was defeated not through force but through cunning: Hermes disguised himself as a shepherd and, through deception and distraction, closed the creature's eyes one by one. The story encodes a durable principle—against an opponent of overwhelming strength, strategy matters more than power.

That principle finds a contemporary application in the effort to defeat stylometric systems and surveillance tools, the many-eyed giants of our moment. Writers who wish to protect their textual privacy must turn to deliberate countermeasures. One such framework is *TraceTarnish*, designed to obscure authorship attribution. This paper evaluates which of its four components—Translation, Obfuscation, Imitation, and Injection—most effectively disrupts stylometric analysis. The results point clearly to Injection: the embedding of zero-width Unicode characters, homoglyphs, and intentional misspellings proves to be the most powerful technique for defeating stylometric detection and preserving authorial anonymity.
target: What did it take for Hermes, the devout messenger of the Olympian gods, to slay Argus Panoptes, the multi-eyed giant of Greek myth? As the perfect guardian, Panoptes' legion of ever-watchful eyes proved difficult -- but not impossible -- to defeat. The centerpiece of Hermes' strategy was obfuscation and sabotage. Posing as a shepherd, Hermes sealed each of Panoptes' eyes -- eyes that would otherwise have alerted the fearsome giant to Hermes' plot -- and vanquished him. The moral of the story: when a challenger must surmount a formidable foe -- one far greater in stature and vastly more equipped -- crafty maneuvers are not merely advisable but indispensable for victory. In this work, the "challenger" is a collective leveraging adversarial tactics to overcome the "multi-eyed giant" of stylometric systems and surveillance apparatuses. To successfully claw back the privacy siphoned by the multi-eyed giant, the challenger must carefully evaluate their plan of attack, $\textit{TraceTarnish}$, and determine what does and does not work to anonymize the authorship of text. To that end, we conduct an ablation study of $\textit{TraceTarnish}$ to better understand which module -- Translation, Obfuscation, Imitation, or Injection -- best confounds a stylometric system. Our results indicate that the most effective approach was Injection, meaning that inserting zero-width Unicode characters, homoglyphs, and intentional misspellings neutralizes the indefatigable eyes long enough to claim the head of the all-seeing giant.

input: Language-model agents take actions through structured tool calls, where each argument carries a different degree of risk. Untrusted input might safely affect some fields—like the text of an email body—but becomes truly hazardous when it can influence others, such as recipients, accounts, commands to be executed, or credentials. Traditional statistical approaches usually enforce risk controls over complete actions all at once, which means that failures concentrated in rare, high-risk fields can slip through undetected when averaged alongside safer arguments. We propose role-stratified per-field conformal risk control—a calibration layer positioned between any per-field detection method and the enforcement of tailored thresholds and risk budgets based on the semantic role of each argument. When a particular role occurs with frequency $p_r$, conventional aggregate certification must assign an effective budget of $αp_r$ to ensure a role-specific risk of $α$; in contrast, our role-stratified approach certifies each sufficiently frequent role on its own with finite-sample guarantees, while extending coverage to rarer roles via joint certification. Experiments on AgentDojo and InjecAgent across six language models show that the observed performance gaps align with our theoretical predictions about this efficiency cost. Our method sustains the tightest role-specific budget compliance across diverse conditions: model swaps, evolving attacks, noisy detectors, gradual data drift, novel tool sets, and adaptive adversaries. It delivers formal per-role guarantees under standard assumptions or after recalibration, together with empirical compliance when data distributions stay stable. These findings indicate that structured tool calls demand certification at the level of semantic roles rather than at the level of the action as a whole.
target: Language-model agents act through structured tool calls whose arguments carry different risks. Untrusted content may safely influence an email body but should not determine a recipient, account, command, or credential. Existing statistical methods typically control risk over the entire action, allowing failures in rare, high-risk fields to be obscured by benign arguments. We introduce role-stratified per-field conformal risk control, a calibration layer that wraps any per-field detector and sets separate thresholds and risk budgets for semantic argument roles. For a role with prevalence $p_r$, aggregate-only certification must use an effective budget of $αp_r$ to guarantee role-specific risk $α$, whereas role-stratified calibration certifies each sufficiently sampled role directly with a finite-sample guarantee; rarer roles are handled by pooled certification. Across AgentDojo and InjecAgent with six language models, the empirical utility gap tracks this predicted price of coarseness, and our method achieves the most consistent role-specific budget compliance under model and attack transfer, detector noise, gradual drift, unseen tool suites, and adaptive attacks. It provides formal per-role guarantees under exchangeability or after recalibration, and empirical compliance under frozen distribution shift. These results suggest that structured tool calls should be certified at the semantic-role level, not the whole action.

input: Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) struggles to gain acceptance in safety-critical fields like robotics and automotive engineering due to the opaque behavior of deep neural networks. This opacity creates obstacles for meeting regulatory standards and establishing trust between humans and automated agents. This paper presents an experimental investigation into making high-performing continuous control DRL systems transparent and understandable. Using the Inverted Pendulum as a test case, the authors implement a policy distillation approach. They take a Twin Delayed DDPG (TD3) agent—a black-box, high-performing continuous control model—and transfer its learned behavior into an interpretable shallow Decision Tree student model. Through physics-informed features and a technique called "Noisy Oracle Rollouts" to create training data, the distilled student matches the performance of the expert teacher agent. A control-theoretic comparison shows an important limitation: converting from continuous to discrete rule-based control produces rapid Bang-Bang switching patterns and creates a stable two-mode oscillation. The experimental findings demonstrate that the system maintains Bounded-Input Bounded-Output (BIBO) stability while offering interpretability at both system-wide and detailed levels, making it suitable for trustworthy autonomous applications.
target: In safety-critical sectors such as robotics and automotive engineering, the deployment of Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) is often hindered by the black-box nature of deep neural networks. This lack of transparency poses significant challenges for regulatory compliance and human-agent trust. This paper presents an experimental study aimed at making high-performance continuous control DRL systems interpretable. A policy distillation framework is implemented using the classic Inverted Pendulum benchmark. A high-performance Twin Delayed DDPG (TD3) agent serves as an opaque, continuous teacher model, whose policy is distilled into an interpretable student surrogate based on a shallow Decision Tree. By leveraging a custom physics-aware feature and "Noisy Oracle Rollouts" for dataset generation, the distillation process achieves performance equivalent to the expert teacher. Furthermore, comparative control theory analysis reveals a fundamental trade-off: transitioning from continuous to discrete rule-based control induces high-frequency Bang-Bang actuation and a stable bimodal limit cycle. Simulation results indicate that Bounded-Input Bounded-Output (BIBO) stability is maintained while providing both global and local interpretability for safe autonomous systems.

input: Bayesian nonparametric (BNP) learning methods designed for large-scale applications, such as Stochastic Variational Inference (SVI), are capable of handling datasets with many classes and large numbers of samples. Like SVI, these approaches generally rely on conjugate variational posteriors to approximate the true posterior distribution. However, adapting this framework to accommodate non-conjugate posteriors is considerably more difficult. While recent work has explored Monte Carlo approximations as a solution, their use has been largely confined to non-BNP tasks and relatively straightforward models such as logistic regression, owing to computational limitations. To overcome these shortcomings of SVI, we propose a new method based on constant stepsize stochastic gradient ascent, which facilitates large-scale learning with non-conjugate posteriors. In contrast to SVI, our approach does not demand closed-form solutions for variational posterior expectations; it requires only that the variational posterior be differentiable. Whereas SVI relies on decaying step-sizes to achieve convergence in stochastic settings, our method employs adaptive stepsizes drawn from principles underlying both SVI and Adam, resulting in meaningful improvements in learning performance. We show that our approach pairs effectively with ResNet features on large-scale datasets, including MIT67 and SUN397. When evaluated against recent methods—including deep clustering algorithms—our learner achieves performance that is comparable to or better than state-of-the-art results on standard clustering benchmarks.
target: Large scale Bayesian nonparametrics (BNP) learner such as Stochastic Variational Inference (SVI) can handle datasets with large class number and large training size at fractional cost. Like its predecessor, SVI rely on the assumption of conjugate variational posterior to approximate the true posterior. A more challenging problem is to consider large scale learning on non-conjugate posterior. Recent works in this direction are mostly associated with using Monte Carlo methods for approximating the learner. However, these works are usually demonstrated on non-BNP related task and less complex models such as logistic regression, due to higher computational complexity. In order to overcome the issue faced by SVI, we develop a novel approach based on the recently proposed constant stepsize stochastic gradient ascent to allow large scale learning on non-conjugate posterior. Unlike SVI, our new learner does not require closed- form expression for the variational posterior expectatations. Our only requirement is that the variational posterior is differentiable. In order to ensure convergence in stochastic settings, SVI rely on decaying step-sizes to slow its learning. Inspired by SVI and Adam, we propose the novel use of adaptive stepsizes in our method to significantly improve its learning. We show that our proposed methods is compatible with ResNet features when applied to large class number datasets such as MIT67 and SUN397. Finally, we compare our proposed learner with several recent works such as deep clustering algorithms and showed we were able to produce on-par or outperform the state-of-the-art methods in terms of clustering measures.

input: Split learning allows neural networks to be trained collaboratively across distributed clients and servers, yet badly selected split points introduce significant privacy risks by leaking sensitive information through intermediate representations. This paper presents a topology-based framework designed to mitigate privacy risks in split learning by analyzing the persistent Betti complexity of activation patterns. Through a layer-by-layer examination, we find that privacy vulnerabilities are not spread evenly throughout networks but rather cluster in specific critical zones that cannot be predicted by network depth alone. Specifically, the vulnerability of features to inversion attacks increases steeply at particular depths, with SSIM values climbing as high as 0.98 at the most exposed split positions. We demonstrate that Betti complexity dependably pinpoints representation states prone to privacy compromise, yielding consistent outcomes across diverse network architectures and training datasets. Building on these findings, we introduce BettiSafe, an automated technique that identifies privacy-vulnerable layers via topological measurements instead of computationally expensive attack simulations. BettiSafe provides 2–5 times greater protection against feature inversion compared to standard depth-based methods while maintaining classification accuracy. In addition, applying Betti-informed regularization makes feature reconstruction about 5 times harder without harming model performance, achieving a favorable trade-off between privacy and utility. Our results demonstrate that topological properties offer a powerful means of constructing split learning systems that are secure, adaptable, and mindful of representation integrity in practical distributed learning settings.
target: Split learning enables collaborative model training by partitioning neural networks across clients and servers. However, improper split placement can lead to severe privacy leakage through intermediate representations. In this work, we propose a topology-guided framework for privacy-aware split learning based on the persistent Betti complexity of smashed activations. Through comprehensive layer-wise analysis, we show that privacy risk in split learning is highly non-uniform across layers and exhibits sharp transition regions that are not captured by architectural depth alone. In particular, feature inversion fidelity increases from negligible reconstruction to as high as 0.98 SSIM at deeper, privacy-critical split points. We further demonstrate that Betti complexity consistently identifies representation regimes associated with elevated feature-space privacy leakage across architectures and datasets. Leveraging this observation, we introduce BettiSafe, a topology-guided split selection strategy that identifies privacy-sensitive layers without requiring explicit attack execution. BettiSafe improves resistance to feature inversion by 2 to 5 times compared to depth-based heuristics while preserving classification accuracy. In addition, Betti-based regularisation increases inversion difficulty by nearly 5 x without degrading model utility, enabling a favourable privacy utility tradeoff. Overall, our results highlight topological complexity as a promising structural descriptor for secure, adaptive, and representation-aware split learning in real-world collaborative systems

input: We investigate a three-dimensional model of charged-particle motion formulated in terms of nonrelativistic momentum and develop a curve-reference exponential integrator (CREI) applicable to it. The linear component of the system has a zero eigenvalue that lacks semisimplicity, which means the system cannot be transformed into a form satisfying the spectral requirements of the standard locally linearized extended exponential integrator (LLEEI). To address this, we decompose the primary magnetic matrix into kernel and range components, then apply an additional linear change of variables. These steps convert the system into an equivalent form featuring a semisimple zero block coupled with a constant skew-symmetric block exhibiting oscillatory behavior. Rather than expanding the nonlinear term around a single fixed point, the CREI performs this expansion along the precise oscillatory solution curve. The variant CREI(k + 1) is obtained by truncating the expansion of the nonlinear term to include all monomials up to degree k. We establish uniform error bounds for both local and global behavior, and we provide repeatable computational results demonstrating convergence with respect to the step size h and uniformity with respect to the parameter ε.
target: We study a three-dimensional charged-particle dynamics model in the nonrelativistic momentum formulation and construct a curve-reference exponential integrator (CREI) for this system. Since the zero eigenvalue of linear section is not semisimple, the system after usual change of variables does not meet the spectral condition used in the classical locally linearized extended exponential integrator (LLEEI). A kernel-range decomposition of the dominant magnetic matrix and a further linear transformation reduce the equation to a system with a semisimple zero block and one constant skew-symmetric oscillatory block. The CREI expands the nonlinear term along the exact oscillatory curve rather than at a fixed point. Retaining monomials through degree k defines CREI(k + 1). We prove uniform local and global error bounds and present reproducible numerical experiments for convergence in h and uniformity in ε.

This paper presents a derivative-based finite volume Hermite WENO (HWENO) scheme for hyperbolic conservation laws. The scheme evolves both the solution and its first-order derivatives simultaneously in time, incorporating both quantities into the spatial reconstruction. A central challenge in solving hyperbolic conservation laws is that discontinuities may emerge in computed solutions. At these discontinuities, derivatives can become unbounded, potentially destabilizing HWENO schemes. The original HWENO method used separate stencil configurations to reconstruct the primary equation and the derivative equation independently, aiming to limit the influence of derivatives while maintaining high-order accuracy. However, this strategy considerably increases computational cost and implementation complexity.

To overcome these limitations, the proposed method omits derivative information from the target cell during spatial reconstruction, instead relying on the same reconstructed polynomial within the time-stepping procedure to govern derivatives. This adjustment enhances robustness relative to traditional HWENO schemes and allows a single unified stencil to be used throughout the derivative-based HWENO framework. The scheme also supports arbitrary positive linear weights that sum to one and maintains a compact stencil width. Numerical experiments verify that the proposed HWENO scheme delivers high-order accuracy, computational efficiency, sharp resolution, and robust performance.
target: In this paper, we propose a derivative-based finite volume Hermite WENO (HWENO) scheme for hyperbolic conservation laws, where both the solution and its first-order derivatives are evolved in time and utilized in spatial reconstructions. The key challenge for solving hyperbolic conservation laws is the possible emergence of discontinuities in the numerical solutions. When facing discontinuities, the derivatives can become excessively large, which may compromise the robustness of HWENO schemes. In the first HWENO scheme, different sets of stencils were adopted for reconstructing the governing equation and the derivative equation, respectively, aiming to reduce the influence of the derivatives while preserving high-order accuracy. However, this approach not only substantially increases computational cost but also introduces considerable algorithmic complexity. To overcome these limitations, we exclude the information of the target cell's derivatives from spatial reconstructions, while employing the same reconstructed polynomial during temporal evolution to limit the derivatives. This strategy enhances the robustness of traditional HWENO schemes and allows unified stencils within the derivative-based HWENO framework. Furthermore, the proposed scheme supports arbitrary positive linear weights that sum to one and maintains a compact stencil. Numerical results demonstrate the high-order accuracy, efficiency, high resolution, and robustness of the proposed HWENO scheme.

input: We present a colored Markov-modulated Brownian motion framework for modeling diffusion-based systems in which newly arriving work interrupts the ongoing task, takes top priority in a stack, and must be completed before any suspended tasks can resume. This preemptive mechanism activates whenever incoming work displaces the task currently in progress—as observed in last-come, first-served queueing disciplines and interrupt-driven computational scheduling—with diffusive behavior representing random fluctuations in processing speed. Colors indicate stack position and task priority, while an underlying phase process, evolving through first-kind transitions that preserve the active color, controls both the drift and volatility within each color category. Second-kind transitions introduce higher colors beginning at random positive launch heights. We employ backward recursion to characterize excursions to higher colors using return matrices and occupation-density kernels. Under hold-and-jump and regulated-base boundary conditions, we obtain stationary distributions with a product-form structure, expressed explicitly through matrix-analytic formulas, and we establish matrix-transform relationships for specific launch-height distributions.
target: We develop a colored Markov-modulated Brownian motion model for diffusion-scale systems in which newly created work preempts the active layer, occupies the top of an ordered stack, and must deplete before suspended work resumes. Such preemption arises whenever new work interrupts whatever is currently active, as in last-come, first-served queues and interrupt-driven scheduling, with diffusive dynamics appropriate when the processing rate itself fluctuates randomly. Colors encode stack position and priority, while a background phase, evolving through first-kind transitions that leave the active color unchanged, controls drift and volatility within each color. Second-kind transitions create higher colors at strictly positive random launch heights. A backward recursion summarizes higher-color excursions through return matrices and occupation-density kernels. We obtain stationary product-form representations under hold-and-jump and regulated-base boundary conventions, given explicitly through matrix-analytic formulae, and give matrix-transform formulas for illustrative launch-height families.

Suppose $(X,Y)$ are independent standard real Gaussian random variables, and suppose $(P\in\mathbb C[X,Y])$ satisfies $\mathbb E!\left(P(X,Y)^m\right)=0$ for all $(m\ge1)$. By introducing complex coordinates $Z=\frac{X+iY}{\sqrt2}$ and $W=\frac{X-iY}{\sqrt2}$, we demonstrate that the monomials appearing in $(P)$ form a strictly one-sided support relative to the weight function $\operatorname{wt}(Z^aW^b)=a-b$. This means that all monomials in $(P)$ possess positive weight, or all possess negative weight. Consequently, for any $(Q\in\mathbb C[X,Y])$, we have $\mathbb E!\left(Q(X,Y)P(X,Y)^m\right)=0$ whenever $(m>°Q)$. This establishes the two-variable Gaussian Moments Conjecture with an explicit threshold of $(m\ge°Q+1)$.

The proof's central technique involves a prime-isolation theorem applicable to exposed faces of $(P)$'s Newton polygon. By applying a $(p)$-adic valuation argument at moment indices $(m=qp)$, we isolate the contribution from a selected face and separate it from all other multinomial terms. Frobenius reduction then requires the constant terms of all positive powers of the corresponding one-variable Laurent polynomial to be zero. The Duistermaat-van der Kallen theorem guarantees that the face exhibits weights of uniform sign, while a two-dimensional convex-geometric argument excludes support containing weights of opposite signs. Together with the established one-variable case and counterexamples for $(n\ge3)$, this characterizes exactly which dimensions satisfy the Gaussian Moments Conjecture.
target: Let $(X,Y)$ be independent standard real Gaussian random variables, and let $(P\in\mathbb C[X,Y])$ satisfy $\mathbb E!\left(P(X,Y)^m\right)=0$ for every $(m\ge1)$. Using the complex coordinates $Z=\frac{X+iY}{\sqrt2}, \qquad W=\frac{X-iY}{\sqrt2},$ we prove that the monomial support of $(P)$ is strictly one-sided with respect to the weight $\operatorname{wt}(Z^aW^b)=a-b$. Thus either every monomial occurring in $(P)$ has positive weight, or every monomial has negative weight. It follows that, for every $(Q\in\mathbb C[X,Y])$, $\mathbb E!\left(Q(X,Y)P(X,Y)^m\right)=0$ whenever $(m>°Q)$. This proves the two-variable Gaussian Moments Conjecture with the explicit threshold $m\ge°Q+1$. The main ingredient is a prime-isolation theorem for exposed faces of the Newton polygon of $(P)$. A $(p)$-adic valuation argument at moment indices of the form $(m=qp)$ separates the contribution of a chosen face from all remaining multinomial strata. Frobenius reduction then forces the constant terms of all positive powers of the associated one-variable Laurent polynomial to vanish. The theorem of Duistermaat and van der Kallen implies that the face has weights of one strict sign, while a planar convex-geometric argument rules out support containing weights of both signs. Combined with the known one-variable case and counterexamples in dimensions $(n\ge3)$, this determines the dimensions in which the Gaussian Moments Conjecture holds.

input: Decoding EEG motor imagery signals is highly challenging because of substantial variability between individuals, which makes it difficult to develop methods that work well universally. We conducted a thorough, standardized assessment of decoding techniques within single sessions across three publicly available datasets: Cho2017 (52 subjects), PhysionetMI (109 subjects), and Zhou2016 (4 subjects). Applying uniform MOABB LeftRightImagery protocols, two frequency bands (8–15 Hz and 8–30 Hz), and a broad set of combinations involving feature extraction, preprocessing, and classification, we produced 216,714 raw evaluation records, which condensed to 44,928, 109,000, and 4,192 subject-level results, respectively. Two techniques—covariance tangent-space projection (cov-tgsp) and Common Spatial Patterns (CSP)—emerged as the most reliable, though their relative performance varied between datasets. On Cho2017, cov-tgsp at 8–30 Hz produced the highest mean accuracy (0.712 ± 0.140), while on Zhou2016, CSP at 8–15 Hz performed better (0.832 ± 0.121). These aggregate results, however, masked considerable individual differences: Cho2017 featured 42 distinct optimal pipelines across its 52 subjects, and PhysionetMI had 93 across its 109 subjects. We then leveraged the benchmark data to build compact pipeline collections of different sizes (K). We evaluated several selection strategies, spanning from a straightforward Top-K Mean method to more sophisticated search-based approaches. Most strategies produced comparable outcomes, with Top-K Mean delivering the most consistently balanced performance. A single universal pipeline recovered 94.2% of the maximum attainable performance in Cho2017 and 81.8% in PhysionetMI; expanding to K = 12 pipelines increased these values to 96.5% and 90.0%, respectively. These results confirm that optimal decoding performance is fundamentally subject-specific, and that this variability can be effectively harnessed through compact pipeline collections to support practical, personalized decoding.
target: Robust EEG motor imagery decoding remains limited by strong inter-individual variability, making it difficult to identify pipelines that generalize across users. We present a large-scale, standardized within-session benchmark of decoding pipelines across three public datasets: Cho2017 (52 subjects), PhysionetMI (109 subjects), and Zhou2016 (4 subjects). Using a common MOABB LeftRightImagery setting, two frequency bands (8-15 Hz and 8-30 Hz), and a broad combination of feature extraction, preprocessing, and classification steps, we analyzed 216,714 raw evaluation rows, which after structured aggregation yielded 44,928, 109,000, and 4,192 subject-level observations respectively. Covariance tangent-space projection (cov-tgsp) and Common Spatial Patterns (CSP) consistently defined the strongest methodological families, though their relative ordering was dataset-dependent. On Cho2017, the best family-level mean accuracy came from cov-tgsp in 8-30 Hz (0.712 +/- 0.140), whereas Zhou2016 favored CSP (0.832 +/- 0.121 in 8-15 Hz). These aggregate rankings concealed substantial subject-level heterogeneity: 42 distinct winning pipelines across 52 Cho2017 subjects, and 93 across 109 PhysionetMI subjects. We then used the benchmark as an empirical performance landscape for building compact portfolios of pipelines of size K. Several construction procedures were compared, including a ranking-based Top-K Mean heuristic and search-based strategies. Results were broadly consistent, with Top-K Mean giving the best trade-off. A single best global pipeline already retained 94.2% of the oracle in Cho2017 and 81.8% in PhysionetMI; at K = 12, oracle retention rose to 96.5% and 90.0%. The landscape is therefore subject-dependent, and this heterogeneity can be exploited through compact portfolios that make personalization more feasible.

input: Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents are increasingly being deployed in safety-critical fields including robotics, autonomous driving, and unmanned aerial vehicles, where unpredictable behavior can result in severe real-world harm. Fuzz testing has recently proven to be an effective approach for probing the intricate state spaces of RL agents and revealing system failures. However, the growing array of RL fuzzing techniques has been evaluated using inconsistent methods, benchmarks, and metrics, making it hard to draw fair comparisons about their relative effectiveness and practical value. To close this gap, we introduce the first thorough, large-scale evaluation of RL fuzzing methods, examining them along four central dimensions: performance, diversity, speed, and real-world relevance. We benchmark five cutting-edge techniques together with a random testing baseline under identical settings across three environments of escalating complexity—MountainCar, BipedalWalker, and CARLA—while also evaluating how effectively fuzzing-discovered failures can be used to enhance agent robustness and aid safety verification. Our findings produce several important insights. For example, output-maximizing methods such as MDPFuzz show stronger performance and efficiency in finding crashes, whereas exploration-focused approaches like SeqDivFuzz are better at surfacing a wider variety of failure cases. Moreover, crashes generated through fuzzing can substantially boost agent resilience and support reliable safety assessments that yield consistent results across techniques. Beyond these empirical findings, we provide practical recommendations for both researchers and practitioners, promoting the joint application of multiple fuzzing strategies and the use of comprehensive diversity metrics to enable more rigorous and practically meaningful evaluation of RL systems.
target: Reinforcement Learning (RL) agents are increasingly deployed in safety-critical domains such as robotics, autonomous driving, and drone control, where unexpected behaviors may lead to severe real-world consequences. Fuzz testing has recently emerged as a promising method for exploring the vast state spaces of RL agents and exposing crashes. Although numerous RL fuzzing methods have been proposed, existing studies often differ in evaluation settings, baselines, and metrics, making it difficult to draw reliable conclusions about their relative effectiveness and practical usefulness. To address this gap, we present the first comprehensive empirical study that systematically evaluates RL fuzzing methods from four complementary perspectives: effectiveness, diversity, efficiency, and practical utility. We benchmark five state-of-the-art methods alongside random testing under unified configurations across three environments of increasing complexity (MountainCar, BipedalWalker, and CARLA), and further assess the downstream usefulness of detected crashes for agent robustness improvement and safety monitoring. Our results reveal several key insights. For instance,throughput-oriented methods like MDPFuzz demonstrate superior effectiveness and efficiency in crash discovery, while methods explicitly designed to encourage exploration like SeqDivFuzz excel at uncovering diverse crash behaviors. We also show that fuzzing-generated crashes can meaningfully improve agent robustness and enable accurate safety monitoring with strong cross-method generalization. Beyond these empirical findings, we distill actionable guidance for both researchers and practitioners, highlighting the benefits of combining complementary fuzzing strategies and adopting multi-level diversity analysis to achieve more comprehensive and practical RL testing.

input: We have developed adaptive multi-domain coupling capabilities for the discontinuous Galerkin framework Trixi.jl, enabling the simultaneous treatment of numerous domains governed by different physical models. The coupling mechanism operates through the transmission of boundary data and customizable coupling operators, which permits the connection of systems with disparate variable sets or substantially different variable counts. This flexibility proves especially valuable when managing hierarchical system structures. A key feature of our approach is the ability to dynamically switch between different complexity levels for coupled systems throughout a simulation, making it well-suited for highly transient phenomena typical in astrophysical applications. The adaptivity criteria are fully customizable, allowing users to tailor them to their specific physical needs. By combining high-complexity and low-complexity models in different regions rather than solving the most sophisticated model everywhere, our coupled-system strategy achieves considerable computational savings with minimal implementation overhead.
target: For the discontinuous Galerkin code Trixi.jl we implement capabilities for adaptively coupling arbitrarily many domains with different physics. The coupling of the systems is realized through the exchange of boundary information and user-definable coupling functions. This gives us the ability to couple systems that do not share a single variable or have a very different number of variables. This is particularly useful when we have a hierarchy of systems. Our implementation is such that we can adaptively select the model of the coupled systems in the course of the simulation. This allows for highly dynamical scenarios as can be found e.g. in astrophysics. The criteria for adaptivity can be user defined and tailored to the physical problem. Compared to computing the most complex model in the entire simulation domain, our method of coupled systems of high and low complexity leads to a significant reduction in computational time with very little overhead.

input: We investigate how compression affects Coordinate Descent Full Configuration Interaction (CDFCI) within an unconstrained optimization approach to the full configuration interaction ground-state problem. Assuming appropriate local conditions, we establish that the compressed iterative method converges linearly toward the solution of a related reduced problem. We further identify the limit point of the compressed algorithm. In the case where the target eigenvector exhibits an additional exponential decay property, we demonstrate that the resulting eigenvalue error behaves like $τ^2$, with $τ$ representing the compression threshold. Numerical experiments validate our theoretical findings.
target: We study the effect of compression in Coordinate Descent Full Configuration Interaction (CDFCI) within an unconstrained optimization formulation of the full configuration interaction ground-state problem. Under suitable local assumptions, we prove that the compressed iteration converges linearly to the solution of an associated restricted problem. We also characterize the convergence point of the compressed algorithm. Under an additional exponential decay assumption on the target eigenvector, we show that the resulting eigenvalue error is of order $τ^2$, where $τ$ denotes the compression threshold. Numerical results support the analysis.

input: We present a goal-oriented error-estimation framework for first-order system least-squares (FOSLS) finite element methods that uses the physical PDE adjoint instead of the adjoint derived from the least-squares formulation. By extracting the physical adjoint directly from the differential operator, its mixed boundary conditions, and the desired output, we obtain a system that possesses its own first-order flux formulation and therefore an inherent least-squares estimator—something the least-squares-induced adjoint lacks. Our error identities are based on a primal-dual corrected functional that depends solely on the continuous primal and adjoint equations, applies to any conforming approximations, and does not rely on Galerkin orthogonality. For outputs involving a weighted Dirichlet-boundary flux, where the weight serves as the key parameter for the adjoint, we develop two corrected approximations: one derived from potentials alone, and another that additionally incorporates fluxes. We establish product-type error estimates relating to both primal and adjoint errors. The least-squares functionals then provide computable a posteriori bounds and a balanced marking indicator in which the sum over all elements equals the product of the two estimators precisely. Computational results validate the expected convergence rates and demonstrate the efficiency of the marking strategy.
target: We develop a goal-oriented error-estimation framework for first-order system least-squares (FOSLS) finite element methods based on the physical PDE adjoint rather than the adjoint induced by the least-squares formulation. Identified explicitly from the differential operator, its mixed boundary conditions, and the output, the physical adjoint admits its own first-order flux system and hence a native, built-in least-squares estimator, which the least-squares-induced adjoint does not. Our error identities rest on a primal-dual corrected functional: they follow from the continuous primal and adjoint equations alone, hold for arbitrary conforming approximations, and require no Galerkin orthogonality. For outputs containing a weighted Dirichlet-boundary flux, whose weight becomes the essential datum of the adjoint, we construct two corrected approximations, one from the potentials and one also using the fluxes, and prove product-type error estimates in the primal and adjoint errors. The least-squares functionals then yield computable a posteriori bounds and a balanced marking indicator whose element sum equals the product of the two estimators exactly. Numerical experiments confirm the predicted convergence and the effectiveness of the marking.
