We study heavy-Wigner tensors: symmetric random tensors whose independent entries (up to tensor symmetries) are mean-zero, with moments that scale as $N^{-(p-1)}$, where $N$ is the tensor dimension. This class includes normalized adjacency tensors of sparse Erdős-Rényi hypergraphs and truncated heavy-tailed tensor models. We investigate trace invariants—a complete family of polynomial invariants that are invariant under permutations of tensor indices. After suitable normalization, we show that asymptotic contributions vanish except for those arising from fat hypertrees, and we prove a central limit theorem for these injective trace invariants.

Our applications are as follows. We first study Erdős-Rényi $p$-uniform hypergraphs with edge probability $\alpha_N = c/N^{p-1}$. We prove local weak convergence to a uniform Galton-Watson hypertree with Poisson offspring distribution. We also show that the empirical spectral distribution of matrices obtained by contracting the adjacency tensor converges: in the sparse regime, the limiting distribution depends on the sparsity parameter $c$ and has unbounded support, while when $N^{p-1}\alpha_N \to \infty$ and $N^{p-1}(1-\alpha_N) \to \infty$, the limiting spectral distribution is the semicircle law. These results extend to matrices arising from contracting arbitrary heavy-Wigner tensors, for which we give an explicit formula for the moments of the limiting spectral measure.
target: We investigate heavy-Wigner tensors: symmetric random tensors whose independent entries, up to the tensor symmetries, are centered and have moments of order $N^{-(p-1)}$, where $N$ is the tensor dimension. This framework includes normalized adjacency tensors of sparse Erdős-Rényi hypergraphs and truncated heavy-tailed tensor models. We study trace invariants, a complete family of polynomial invariants under permutations of the tensor indices. We prove that, after the natural normalization, the only non-vanishing asymptotic contributions are those associated with fat hypertrees, and we derive a central limit theorem for these injective trace invariants. As applications, we first analyze Erdős-Rényi $p$-uniform hypergraphs with edge probability $α_N=c/N^{p-1}$. We prove local weak convergence to a uniform Galton-Watson hypertree with Poisson offspring distribution. We also prove convergence of the empirical spectral distribution of the matrix obtained by contracting the adjacency tensor; in the sparse regime the limiting law depends on the sparsity parameter $c$ and has unbounded support, while in the regime $N^{p-1}α_N\to\infty$ with $N^{p-1}(1-α_N)\to\infty$, the limiting spectral distribution is the semicircle law. This result generalizes for matrices obtained by contracting an arbitrary heavy-Wigner tensor and we derive an explicit formula for the moments of the limiting spectral measure.

input: The totally asymmetric simple exclusion process (TASEP) with open boundaries is a finite Markov chain where particles jump between neighboring sites on a one-dimensional lattice, with the dynamics at the left and right boundaries controlled by parameters $\alpha$ and $\beta$. In the multispecies variant of TASEP, particles carry distinct species labels. Ferrari and Martin (2007) proposed multiline queues as a means of computing the stationary distribution of multispecies TASEP on a periodic lattice. However, obtaining a combinatorial formula for the stationary distribution in the open-boundary multispecies TASEP case has remained unsolved. We address this by employing Kirillov--Reshetikhin crystals of type $C$ to define type $C$ multiline queues, along with an accompanying Ferrari--Martin pairing algorithm that maps these queues to TASEP configurations. This construction produces a combinatorial formula for the stationary distribution of multispecies open-boundary TASEP in the special case $\alpha = \beta = 1$.
target: The totally asymmetric simple exclusion process (TASEP) with open boundaries is a finite Markov chain describing particles hopping between adjacent sites on a one-dimensional lattice with left and right boundary transitions governed by parameters $α$ and $β$. The multispecies TASEP is a higher-rank generalization in which particles have different species. Multiline queues were introduced by Ferrari and Martin (2007) to compute the stationary distribution of the multispecies TASEP on a circle. It has remained an open problem to find a combinatorial formula for the stationary distribution of the multispecies open-boundary TASEP. Using Kirillov--Reshetikhin crystals of type $C$, we construct type $C$ multiline queues and a corresponding Ferrari--Martin pairing algorithm that projects them to TASEP configurations. This yields a combinatorial formula for the stationary distribution of the multispecies open-boundary TASEP for the $α=β=1$ specialization.

input: When the infinite Robinson-Schensted-Knuth (RSK) correspondence is applied to a sequence of independent, uniformly distributed random variables on [0,1], it produces the Plancherel-random infinite Young tableau. We build upon previously established dynamical systems isomorphisms to give an explicit geometric description of the inverse transformation. Our method employs a novel structure—the jeu de taquin forest defined on the infinite tableau—in which boxes are linked by edges following local comparison rules. We demonstrate that, with probability one, each forest tree grows infinitely with a well-defined limiting direction, thereby creating a canonical correspondence between trees and the entries of the original i.i.d. input sequence. The original sequence order is then reconstructed by examining how long each tree persists under repeated jeu de taquin operations.
target: The Plancherel-random infinite Young tableau arises from applying the infinite Robinson-Schensted-Knuth (RSK) correspondence to a sequence of i.i.d. random variables distributed uniformly on the unit interval [0,1]. Building on the isomorphism of dynamical systems established in prior work, we provide an explicit geometric characterization of the inverse map. Our approach makes use of a previously unexplored structure, the jeu de taquin forest on the infinite tableau, where edges connect boxes according to local comparison rules. We prove that each tree in this forest almost surely extends toward infinity with a well-defined asymptotic direction, establishing a canonical bijection between trees and values in the i.i.d. input sequence. The ordering is recovered through tree lifetimes under iterated jeu de taquin transformations.

input: The electroencephalogram (EEG) serves as an important and extensively utilized instrument for diagnosing brain disorders and examining behavioral modifications. It provides a minimally intrusive and non-invasive approach to investigation. Nevertheless, obstacles arise when applying EEG to research cognitive development, particularly regarding temporal resolution, source localization of signals, and EEG artifact contamination. Thoughtful evaluation of these elements is critical for the proper and effective deployment of EEG technology. Independent component analysis (ICA) successfully separates individual source generator activities from data collected through multiple adjacent scalp electrodes. While ICA decomposition necessitates hands-on examination, curation, and analysis of independent components (ICs)—a labor-intensive undertaking requiring specialized knowledge—automated IC classification can provide adequate precision. This automation accelerates investigations at scale and facilitates immediate feedback during brain activity filtering operations, which are vital for clinical practitioners. This work presents an automated visual computing-based tool for ICA artifact identification that integrates seamlessly with established platforms such as ICLabel and EEGLab. By replacing the manual classification procedure, the developed system decreases analysis time by 7200-fold while maintaining 89.45% accuracy.
target: The electroencephalogram (EEG) is a valuable and widely applied tool for investigating brain disorders and behavioral changes. It offers a minimally restrictive and non-invasive method. However, challenges in using EEG for cognitive development studies include temporal resolution, signal source localization, and EEG artifacts. Careful consideration of these factors is essential for informed application of EEG technology. Independent component analysis (ICA) effectively isolates source generator processes from signals recorded by multiple, adjacent EEG scalp electrodes. Although ICA decomposition requires manual inspection, selection, and interpretation of independent components (ICs), this process is time consuming and demands expertise. Automated IC classification can achieve sufficient accuracy, expediting large scale EEG research and enabling near real time applications in conjunction with brain activity rejection tasks, which are crucial for medical specialists. This study introduces an automated computer vision based ICA rejection labeling tool compatible with widely used software interfaces like ICLabel and EEGLab. By automating the manual task, the proposed system reduces processing time by 7200 fold and achieves an accuracy of 89.45%.

input: Machine translation for low-resource languages such as Tamil presents substantial challenges, stemming from scarce parallel corpora, broad domain variation, and intricate morphological complexity. This study offers a comprehensive evaluation of how multiple multilingual translation models handle English-to-Tamil and Tamil-to-English translation tasks across four datasets: NTREX, EnTamV2, WikiMatrix, and PMIndia. Supervised neural machine translation systems—namely NLLB and mBART—are assessed using both BLEU and chrF metrics to gauge performance across datasets that differ in quality and domain scope. Using attention-based analysis, the study improves model interpretability by mapping token alignments between English source text and Tamil output, providing insight into the underlying translation process. The study further shows that in-context prompting allows the Tamil-capable TamilLLaMA model to perform effective few-shot translation between English and Tamil, with its outputs qualitatively compared against those of supervised approaches. Findings suggest that dataset quality and domain relevance play a decisive role in model performance, that attention mechanisms contribute meaningfully to explainability, and that few-shot large language models are capable of generating structurally coherent Tamil translations.
target: The challenge of Machine Translation for low resource languages such as Tamil is primarily caused by the restricted amount of parallel data for these languages, as well as their substantial amount of domain variation and morphological complexity. This research presents the comprehensive evaluation of the performance of several multilingual translation models on English-Tamil and Tamil-English translations across multiple datasets: NTREX, EnTamV2, WikiMatrix and PMIndia. This study evaluates supervised NMT systems, NLLB and mBART, using both the BLEU and chrF metric, and examines how these systems perform on data of different quality levels and domains. This performs an attention-based analysis to increase model interpretability by visualising the alignments of tokens in an English source text and their Tamil translations and vice-versa to provide insight into how they make translations. This study also demonstrates that using in-context prompting can provide an excellent way to perform a few-shot translation of English to Tamil and Tamil-English using a Tamil capable TamilLaMA model, and compare this to supervised approaches qualitatively. These findings show that the quality of the datasets and their alignment with the domain will greatly affect the performance of the model, that attention-based mechanisms can aid in explain ability, and that few-shot large language models can still produce structurally coherent translations of Tamil.

input: We investigate a simplified framework for learning distributions from constrained conditional samples, motivated by scenarios involving heterogeneous and overlapping data sources. The problem is to infer an unknown distribution $p$ defined over a finite domain $[n]$. A learner has access to a predetermined collection of queryable sets $\mathscr{S} \subseteq 2^{[n]}$, where querying $S \in \mathscr{S}$ yields an independent draw from $p(\cdot \mid S)$. The structure of the co-occurrence graph induced by $\mathscr{S}$ determines learning feasibility: elements are connected if they coappear in at least one queryable set. When this graph is connected on the support of the target distribution, pointwise consistency becomes achievable. PAC learning imposes stronger requirements: success demands that the co-occurrence graph be complete. Sample complexity for PAC learning ranges from near-linear to quadratic. Any query family with a complete co-occurrence graph requires at most $\widetilde O(n^2/ε^2)$ samples, and this is worst-case optimal. Conversely, when all of $[n]$ is queryable, standard sampling achieves $Θ(n/ε^2)$ samples, and no strategy can improve beyond this even with arbitrary query families. More broadly, we show that hierarchical comparability is a sufficient structural property of $\mathscr S$ yielding near-linear optimal complexity $\widetilde Θ(n/ε^2)$, exemplified by pairwise query families. Finally, all polynomial rates between linear and quadratic are achievable: for any $α\in (1,2)$, there exists a query family whose optimal PAC rate is $\widetilde Θ(n^α/ε^2)$.
target: Motivated by learning from heterogeneous and overlapping data providers, we study a stylized model of distribution learning from restricted conditional samples. The goal is to learn an unknown distribution $p$ on a finite domain $[n]$. The learner is given a fixed family of queryable sets $\mathscr{S} \subseteq 2^{[n]}$, and each query to $S \in \mathscr{S}$ returns an independent sample from the conditional distribution $p(\cdot \mid S)$. Learnability is governed by the co-occurrence graph associated with $\mathscr{S}$: two domain elements are adjacent if they appear together in some queryable set. Pointwise consistency is achievable when this graph is connected on the target support. PAC learning requires more: it is possible when the co-occurrence graph is complete. The optimal sample complexity of PAC learning ranges from nearly linear to quadratic. Every query family with complete co-occurrence graph admits sample complexity $\widetilde O(n^2/ε^2)$, and this bound is tight in the worst case. On the other hand, if $[n]$ is queryable then ordinary sampling improves the bound to $Θ(n/ε^2)$, and this cannot be improved further even if every set is queryable. More generally, we identify hierarchical comparabilityas a sufficient structural condition on $\mathscr S$ under which the optimal complexity is nearly linear, $\widetilde Θ(n/ε^2)$, with pairwise query families as a canonical example. Finally, the full range of polynomial rates between linear and quadratic is attainable: for every $α\in (1,2)$, there exists a query family with optimal PAC rate $\widetilde Θ(n^α/ε^2)$.

input: Leveraging multiple data modalities for classification tasks offers complementary information from varied sources, thereby enhancing prediction accuracy. However, real-world deployments frequently face operational obstacles—such as hardware failures or data privacy constraints—that result in discrepancies between the modalities available during training and those available at inference time. Although prior work has largely focused on bimodal settings by designing more robust fusion strategies, we introduce an alternative framework grounded in multi-modal co-learning that prioritizes inter-modal collaboration over integration. Our approach supports any combination of absent modalities without making assumptions about which specific modalities will be missing at deployment—a condition we refer to as arbitrary missing modalities. To address this challenge, we propose two complementary solutions operating at the feature level and the decision level, respectively. Experiments conducted on two multi-modal classification benchmarks demonstrate significant gains in robustness across varying missing modality conditions. The first solution performs best when only a small number of modalities are absent (specifically one), whereas the second solution is better suited to cases of severe modality scarcity (where only a single modality remains available). Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/fmenat/Co4Miss.
target: Multi-modal classification leverages complementary information across diverse data sources to enhance predictive performance. However, real-world scenarios subject to operational constraints, such as sensor failures or privacy restrictions, lead to inconsistent modality availability between training and inference times. To handle missing modalities, prior studies have mainly covered bimodal data setups and focused on designing robust fusion processes. Instead, we adopt a multi-modal co-learning framework that prioritizes inter-modal collaboration rather than multi-modal fusion. Specifically, we consider that any subset of modalities may be absent, without assuming predefined missing-modality patterns, an inference scenario we refer to as missing arbitrary modalities. To address this challenge, we introduce two alternative approaches that leverage information at both feature- and decision-level. Experiments on two multi-modal classification benchmarks demonstrate significant robustness gains in various missing modality conditions. The first method shows more robust behavior under minimal missing conditions, where a single modality is absent, whereas the second performs better under extreme missing conditions, where all-but-one modalities are missing. Our code is available at https://github.com/fmenat/Co4Miss.

input: An anchored active-stage formulation produces a family of implicit one-step methods of arbitrary order that use two derivatives. At each node, both the vector field and its first total time derivative are evaluated, enriching the local Hermite data while holding the number of unknown stage states fixed. The method anchors the initial value and introduces $s$ unknown active stages; $2s$ Hermite moment conditions then achieve global order $2s$. The two remaining coefficients in each stage row are taken from the second-subdiagonal Padé approximant $[s-1/s+1]_{e^z}$. For any ordered real node set, a Padé–Hermite basis theorem establishes that the resulting closure is unique, preserves all moment conditions, satisfies $\det(I-zA-z^2\widehat A)=Q_s(z)$ and $R_s(z)=P_s(z)/Q_s(z)$, introduces no hidden poles into the coupled stage system, and produces an $L$-stable (and hence $A$-stable) one-step map for every positive integer $s$. Symbolic verification covers cases through $s=6$, and high-precision computation confirms orders $2, 4, 6,$ and $8$ for the first four instances. When benchmarked against Gauss–Legendre and Radau IIA methods at the same active-stage count, the construction delivers both higher accuracy at high order and reliable stiff damping across a wide range of step sizes.
target: An arbitrary-order family of implicit two-derivative one-step methods is constructed in an anchored active-stage formulation. At each information node the method uses both the vector field and its first total time derivative, enriching the local Hermite data without increasing the number of unknown stage states. With the known initial value retained as an anchor and $s$ unknown active stages, $2s$ Hermite moment conditions yield global order $2s$. The two remaining coefficients in each stage row are fixed by the second-subdiagonal Padé approximant $[s-1/s+1]_{e^z}$. For every ordered real node set, a Padé--Hermite basis theorem proves that the closure is unique, preserves all moment conditions, and gives $\det(I-zA-z^2\widehat A)=Q_s(z)$ and $R_s(z)=P_s(z)/Q_s(z)$. Hence the coupled stage system has no hidden poles and the accepted one-step map is $L$-stable (and therefore $A$-stable) for every positive integer $s$. Exact symbolic verification is reported through $s=6$, and high-precision computations confirm orders $2,4,6,$ and $8$ for the first four members. At equal active-stage count, comparisons with Gauss--Legendre and Radau IIA methods demonstrate the combined high-order accuracy and strong stiff damping of the construction over broad step-size ranges.

input: We investigate optimal control problems arising from a stationary reaction–diffusion equation modeling the spatial distribution of tumor cells governed by Gompertz growth dynamics. The treatment variable $m(x)$ serves as a control that kills cells at a rate proportional to their density and is subject to $L^{1}$–$L^{\infty}$ constraints. In the case where the intrinsic growth rate is spatially constant, we demonstrate that applying uniform treatment across the whole domain is the unique optimal solution for the minimization problem. For the maximization problem, we establish that every optimal control has bang-bang structure. Moreover, in one spatial dimension with sufficiently strong diffusion, we characterize the support of optimal controls as an interval touching the boundary of the domain. We complement these theoretical findings with numerical experiments that examine regimes beyond the scope of our analysis. These simulations verify the bang-bang nature of maximizers and demonstrate how spatial variation in growth rates, restrictions on the allowable treatment region, and the strength of diffusion together affect both the optimal controls and the associated cell distributions. In particular, the simulations uncover a monotonic relationship between the optimized population size and diffusion strength—a property that contrasts with what is seen in logistic growth models.
target: We study optimal control problems for a stationary reaction--diffusion model describing the spatial distribution of a tumor cell population with Gompertz growth. The control $m(x)$ represents a treatment term acting as a density-dependent removal rate and it is subject to $L^{1}-L^{\infty}$ constraints. When the intrinsic growth rate is constant, the uniform distribution of the treatment is shown to be the unique minimizer. For the maximization problem, we prove that every optimal control is of bang-bang type. In addition, we show that in the one dimensional case and for sufficiently large diffusion rates, the positivity set of optimal controls is an interval sticking to one of the extrema of the domain. Finally, numerical simulations complement the theoretical analysis and explore regimes that are not fully covered by the results proved in the paper. The computations confirm the bang-bang structure of maximizers, and illustrate how the shape of optimal controls and the associated states are affected by spatial heterogeneity in the growth rate, localized admissible treatment regions, and the diffusion coefficient. Moreover, they reveal a monotone dependence of the optimized total population on the diffusion coefficient: this is a new phenomenon with respect to the logistic setting.

input: Phase separation in complex fluids is known to respond sensitively to hydrodynamic effects. During spinodal decomposition of a binary fluid mixture, the resulting domain pattern is shaped not only by interfacial dynamics but also by advection. In certain applications, advection can even trigger turbulence, which in turn influences segregation across multiple spatial scales. To address this, we introduce a Cahn-Hilliard model incorporating transport noise that accounts for the inherent randomness present in turbulent flows. We analyze this model within a thermodynamically-consistent setting that includes a singular Flory-Huggins potential and potentially degenerate mobility, treating the noise in both Ito and Stratonovich interpretations. As an initial study, we demonstrate the well-posedness of the system in two and three spatial dimensions and verify its thermodynamic consistency.
target: Phase separation phenomena occurring in complex fluids are known to be sensitive to hydrodynamic effects: when a binary fluid mixture undergoes spinodal decomposition, the emerging pattern of domains is no longer dictated by interfacial dynamics alone, but is reshaped by advection. In several applications of interest, advection effects may even cause the onset of turbulence, further affecting the segregation process on a wide range of spatial scales. Motivated by this, we propose a Cahn-Hilliard model driven by transport noise able to capture the intrinsic stochasticity of turbulence. The model is analyzed in its thermodynamically-relevant framework, namely employing a singular Flory-Huggins potential and a possibly degenerate mobility, and the noise is considered both in Ito and Stratonovich form. In this work, as a first-step investigation, we establish well-posedness of the system in two and three spatial dimensions and its thermodynamical consistency.

Let $(X_1,\ldots,X_n)$ be independent nonnegative random variables with $\mathbb{E} X_i\le1$, and define $S=\sum_iX_i$. We prove that for any $\delta>0$,

$$\mathbb{P}\left(S<\mathbb{E} S+\delta\right)\ge b_{n,\delta},$$

where $b_{n,\delta}=\delta(n/(n+\delta))^n$ for $0<\delta<1$ and $b_{n,\delta}=(1-1/(n+\delta))^n$ for $\delta\ge1$. This bound is tight for all $n$ and $\delta\ge 1$. In particular, since $b_{n,\delta} \ge e^{-1}$ whenever $\delta\ge 1$, our result confirms Feige's conjecture [Feige, 2004] in the regime $\delta\ge 1$. The proof draws on the exact Dirichlet calibration theorem of Vlassis and Thomas [Vlassis and Thomas, 2026], which resolves Gaffke's conjecture in statistics, together with tools from convex geometry, namely Grünbaum's centroid theorem [Grünbaum, 1960] and its generalization by Letwin and Yaskin [Letwin and Yaskin, 2024]. The proof was discovered by ChatGPT 5.6 Pro.

The bound is sharp for every $n$ and $δ\ge 1$. In particular, since $b_{n,δ} \ge e^{-1}$ for $δ\ge 1$, our result proves Feige's conjecture [Feige, 2004] in the affirmative for $δ\ge 1$. The proof is found by ChatGPT 5.6 Pro. It combines the exact Dirichlet calibration theorem of Vlassis and Thomas [Vlassis and Thomas, 2026], which resolves Gaffke's conjecture in statistics, with results in convex geometry including Grünbaum's centroid theorem [Grünbaum, 1960] and its generalization by Letwin and Yaskin [Letwin and Yaskin, 2024].

Entity matching refers to the task of identifying records that correspond to the same real-world entity. Language models can be applied to entity matching using three main approaches: bi-encoder, cross-encoder, and generative matcher architectures. Unfortunately, previous research frequently combines variations in matcher architecture with differences in model backbone, model variant (stemming from different pretraining approaches), and model size, making it challenging to determine which factors drive performance improvements. 

To overcome this limitation, we conducted a systematic factorial study that isolates these variables. Our investigation examined three matcher architectures, three model variants, and three model sizes from the Qwen3 family, applied to nine datasets, resulting in 1,215 fine-tuning experiments. We additionally assessed how models transfer across datasets and measured computational requirements.

Our findings reveal that model variant plays a crucial role in bi-encoder performance: variants designed for embeddings provide better starting points and produce representation spaces that correlate with matching success. Cross-encoders consistently outperform bi-encoders because they process record pairs together rather than separately, though this advantage narrows somewhat with larger models. Generative matchers do not consistently beat cross-encoders; rather, they excel specifically when data distribution shifts, such as when record schemas differ unexpectedly or when transferring between datasets. We also discovered that larger models tend to rely on shortcut learning patterns and therefore do not always achieve better results.

These insights clarify what drives performance differences among matcher types and suggest that future studies and benchmarks should better separate architectural decisions from model-specific factors while paying greater attention to distribution shifts and cross-dataset performance. Our experimental results, code, training scripts, and evaluation datasets are available at https://github.com/Jantory/llm-trained-matcher.
target: Entity matching identifies records that refer to the same real-world entity. However, prior studies often conflate matcher architecture with differences in model backbone, model variant(reflecting different pretraining objectives), and model size, making it difficult to isolate the sources of performance gains. We address this issue through a controlled factorial study spanning three matcher architectures, three model variants and three model sizes from the Qwen3 family, and nine datasets, totaling 1,215 fine-tuning runs. We also evaluate cross-dataset transferability and computational cost. Our results show that model variant is critical for bi-encoders: embedding-oriented variants provide stronger initialization and more favorable representation geometry predictive of downstream matching performance. Cross-encoders retain a consistent advantage over bi-encoders because they jointly encode record pairs rather than representing each record independently, although larger models partially narrow this gap. Generative matchers do not universally outperform cross-encoders. Instead, their advantages concentrate under distribution shift, including subtle unseen differences in record schemas and cross-dataset transfer. We further find that larger models rely more heavily on shortcut learning and therefore do not necessarily perform better. These findings clarify the factors underlying performance differences across matcher architectures and motivate future research and benchmark designs that better disentangle architectural choices from model-level factors while explicitly evaluating distribution shift and cross-dataset transferability. We release our experimental results, code, training scripts, and evaluation data at https://github.com/Jantory/llm-trained-matcher.

input: We investigate a one-dimensional eikonal equation incorporating both nonlocal and nonlinear effects, with no constraints imposed on the sign of the spatial gradient. The model operates under minimal regularity conditions for both the nonlocal velocity field and the initial conditions. We introduce a periodic formulation of this model and develop a semi-implicit explicit (IMEX) numerical scheme for its approximation. The proposed scheme is shown to maintain a discrete gradient entropy bound, and we demonstrate its convergence through viscosity solutions. Numerical experiments are provided to demonstrate the model's qualitative features and assess the scheme's computational effectiveness.
target: In this work, we study a one-dimensional nonlocal and nonlinear eikonal equation without sign restriction on its spatial gradient. The equation is characterized by weak regularity assumptions on both the nonlocal velocity field and the initial data. We derive a periodic version of this model and propose a semi-explicit (IMEX) scheme for its numerical approximation. We prove that the scheme preserves a discrete gradient entropy estimate and establish its convergence in the viscosity sense. Finally, we present numerical results illustrating the behavior of the model and the performance of the proposed scheme.

input: In the high-dimensional setting of critical Bernoulli bond percolation on $\Z^d$, we establish that the rescaled empirical measure associated with the cluster containing the origin converges, in an appropriate $σ$-finite framework, to the total occupation measure of super-Brownian motion. By combining this measure convergence with a uniform lower bound on the mass of the critical cluster with respect to the extrinsic (Euclidean) distance—itself a result of independent significance that we establish—we obtain convergence of the rescaled cluster as a compact set under the Hausdorff metric. This permits us to derive the precise one-arm asymptotics $r^2\,\bP(0\leftrightarrow \partial B_r)\to θ_1\in(0,\infty)$, thereby strengthening a theorem of Kozma and Nachmias.
target: For critical Bernoulli bond percolation on $\Z^d$ in the high-dimensional regime, we prove that the rescaled empirical measure of the cluster of the origin converges, in a suitable $σ$-finite sense, to the total occupation measure of super-Brownian motion. Combined with a uniform lower mass bound for the critical cluster with respect to the extrinsic (Euclidean) metric, which we also prove and which is of independent interest, the measure convergence further yields the convergence of the rescaled cluster as a compact set, in the Hausdorff metric. As a consequence, we are able to obtain the sharp one-arm asymptotics $r^2\,\bP(0\leftrightarrow \partial B_r)\to θ_1\in(0,\infty)$, hence refining a result of Kozma and Nachmias.

input: We study the strong convergence rate of the Euler-Maruyama scheme for additive stochastic differential equations driven by fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter $H \in (0,1)$. Assuming a Lipschitz condition on the drift coefficient, we prove convergence rates of $1$ when $H \in (1/2,1)$ and $1/2+H-\varepsilon$ for arbitrarily small $\varepsilon>0$ when $H \in (0,1/2]$. A key ingredient of the proof is a displaced sewing lemma in the stochastic setting, which exploits the conditional Gaussian structure of fractional Brownian motion to control the errors introduced by discretizing the noise in time.
target: We study the strong convergence rate of the Euler-Maruyama scheme for additive stochastic differential equations driven by a fractional Brownian motion with Hurst parameter $H \in (0,1)$. Assuming the drift coefficient to be Lipschitz continuous, we show that the rate is $1$ if $H \in (1/2,1)$, and $1/2+H-\varepsilon$, for any $\varepsilon>0$, if $H \in (0,1/2]$. The main ingredient is a shifted stochastic sewing argument, which exploits the conditional Gaussian structure of fractional Brownian motion to control the noise discretization error.

input: A well-known result in high-dimensional statistical theory is that a fixed aspect ratio—characterized by the limit $n/d\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$ as both the sample size $n$ and the dimension $d$ tend to infinity—is central to describing the fundamental performance limits of classical estimation tasks. A canonical example is recovering the leading eigenvector of a $d\times d$ population covariance matrix from $n$ independent samples: the BBP phase transition identifies a precise threshold, given as a simple function of the aspect ratio, below which the top sample principal component is asymptotically uncorrelated with the true eigenvector, and above which this correlation is strictly positive. This paper demonstrates, in contrast, that online (streaming) algorithms exhibit a fundamentally different behavior, and that a fixed aspect ratio does not suffice to obtain nonzero overlap. We analyze Oja's algorithm, the standard approach for online PCA. Concretely, for the model $\Sigma=\theta^2 v_0v_0^\top+I\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$, where Oja's algorithm is run with step size $\delta/d$ over $n$ iid samples $X_k\sim\mathcal{N}(0,\Sigma)$ to yield the estimate $\hat{v}_n$, we prove a phase transition in the regime $n,d\to\infty$ with $n/d\log d\to\gamma\in(0,\infty)$. The correlation $|\langle\hat{v}_n,v_0\rangle|$ tends to zero when $\gamma<\gamma_*$ and converges to $\rho_*$ when $\gamma>\gamma_*$. The critical threshold and the limiting correlation are given explicitly by $\rho_*=\rho_*(\theta,\delta)=\sqrt{(\theta^2-\delta/2)_+/\theta^2(1+\delta/2)}$ and $\gamma_*=\gamma_*(\theta,\delta)=1/2\delta(\theta^2-\delta/2)_+$. Exactly at the critical point, when $n=\lfloor\gamma_* d\log d+\eta d\rfloor$ as $d\to\infty$ for a fixed $\eta\in\mathbb{R}$, the correlation is itself random: $|\langle\hat{v}_n,v_0\rangle|\stackrel{w}{\to}\rho_*|G|\exp(\eta/2\gamma_*)/\sqrt{\rho_*^4+G^2\exp(\eta/\gamma_*)}$ where $G\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$. This differs markedly from standard high-dimensional PCA, where a constant sample-to-dimension ratio is already enough for nonzero overlap, which subsequently grows monotonically as $n/d$ increases.
target: High dimensional statistical theory has established the importance of constant aspect ratio, when the number of dimensions ($d$) and samples ($n$) satisfy $n,d\to\infty$ with $n/d\to γ\in(0,\infty)$, in understanding the limits of canonical estimation problems. In particular, for estimating the top eigenvector of a $d\times d$ population covariance matrix from $n$ iid samples, the BBP phase transition gives a precise threshold -- a simple functional of the aspect ratio -- such that the top sample principal component attains nonzero asymptotic correlation with the truth only when the leading population eigenvalue exceeds it. In this paper, we show that for online / streaming algorithms the story is very different, and constant aspect ratio is insufficient for nonzero overlap. We study Oja's algorithm, the most popular method for online PCA. Let $Σ=θ^2 v_0v_0^\top+I\in\mathbb{R}^{d\times d}$, and run Oja's algorithm with step size $δ/d$ on $n$ iid samples $X_k\sim\mathcal{N}(0,Σ)$, with output $\hat v_n$. Then, as $n,d\to\infty$ with $n/d\log d\toγ\in(0,\infty)$, we establish a phase transition: $|\langle\hat v_n,v_0\rangle|\to 0$ when $γ<γ_*$, and $\toρ_*$ when $γ>γ_*$. Here $ρ_*=ρ_*(θ,δ)=\sqrt{(θ^2-δ/2)_+/θ^2(1+δ/2)}$ and $γ_*=γ_*(θ,δ)=1/2δ(θ^2-δ/2)_+$. Further, at criticality, when $n=[γ_*d\log d+ηd]$ and $d\to\infty$, $η\in\mathbb{R}$, the correlation is random: $|\langle\hat v_n,v_0\rangle|\stackrel{w}{\to}ρ_*|G|\exp(η/2γ_*)/\sqrt{ρ_*^4+G^2\exp(η/γ_*)}$ where $G\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1)$. This is in stark contrast to ordinary high dimensional PCA, where nonzero overlap is possible at constant $n/d$ and improves as $n/d$ increases.

input: We present a novel approach to coupling Rulkov neural maps and offer a heuristic biological explanation for what happens when perturbations affecting the slow variables become non-negligible. Through analytical methods, we demonstrate that this coupling maintains bounded dynamics and preserves snap-back repellers (which generate Devaney chaos via the Marotto theorem) when these features exist in the uncoupled system. Numerical investigations of two coupled standard chaotic Rulkov maps reveal the emergence of a global strange attractor; its fractal characteristics are indicated by calculations showing a non-integer Kaplan-Yorke dimension. We also conduct conventional numerical analyses examining time series behavior, Lyapunov exponent spectra, bifurcation structure, and attraction basins. In conclusion, we outline how this coupling scheme can be extended to networks comprising any number of neurons.
target: We introduce a novel coupling of Rulkov neural maps, proposing a heuristic biological interpretation for the transition to non-small values of the perturbations acting on the slow variables. We analytically prove that the coupling preserves boundedness of motion and the existence of a snap-back repeller (leading to Devaney chaos by the Marotto theorem), if they are associated to the original system. For the coupling of two standard chaotic Rulkov maps, we present numerical simulations for the orbits of the system showing the arising of a global strange attractor, whose fractal structure is strongly suggested by the computation of a non-integer Kaplan-Yorke dimension. Furthermore, we perform standard numerical studies concerning time series, Lyapunov exponents spectra, bifurcation diagrams and basins of attraction. Finally, we briefly propose a generalization of the coupling to an arbitrary number of neurons.

input: Recent studies have demonstrated that numerous animal species use a two-nostril 'stereo' sense of smell. This paper presents preliminary theoretical calculations examining the conditions under which stereo olfaction provides advantages over single-nostril 'mono' olfaction. Our findings indicate that stereo olfaction is beneficial when odour concentration exhibits substantial relative variation and when air correlations span large spatial scales, particularly within boundary layers close to surfaces. Consequently, stereo olfaction proves most valuable when animals are pinpointing olfactory boundaries on surfaces—for instance, when tracking scent trails.
target: Recent works have highlighted the use of dual nostril 'stereo' olfaction by a variety of animals. In this work we perform "back of the envelope" calculations to determine when stereo olfaction is useful compared to single nostril 'mono' olfaction. We find that stereo olfaction is advantageous when there are large relative changes in the odour concentration, and when the spatial length scales of correlations in air are large, such as in the boundary layer near surfaces. In other words, stereo olfaction is useful when animals are searching surfaces for olfactory edges, such as when tracking odour trails.

input: Let $V$ and $U$ be two independent standard normal random variables. For any Borel measurable function $φ\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, we define $Y_φ=φ(V)+U$, along with $P_φ(y)=\mathbb{E}[V\mid Y_φ=y]$ and $F_φ(x)=\mathbb{E}[P_φ(x+U)]$. We establish that whenever $φ(v)$ is a maximiser of the expression $x(v-F_φ(x))$ with respect to $x\in\mathbb{R}$ for all $v\in\mathbb{R}$, then $φ$ must be the identity function. This result characterises the normalised single-period Kyle (1985) insider trading model. Consequently, Kyle's affine strategy in closed form represents the sole equilibrium strategy in the model under any Gaussian location-scale specifications, and the associated competitive pricing rule must be linear. This resolves a classical open problem in financial economics. Earlier work by Boulatov, Kyle and Livdan (2005, 2013) applied methods from complex analysis to this question. McLennan, Monteiro and Tourky (2017) subsequently obtained a linear growth bound on $P_φ$, showed that $F_φ$ is real-entire, and proved uniqueness under the assumption that any equilibrium strategy coincides locally with a uniquely continuable analytic function. Our approach imposes no regularity condition on $φ$ beyond Borel measurability. The proof employs real-variable and probabilistic methods: the optimisation constraint forces matching upper and lower bounds for Gaussian-randomised monotone functions, with equality holding only for the identity function.
target: Let $V$ and $U$ be independent standard normal random variables. For any Borel map $φ\colon\mathbb{R}\to\mathbb{R}$, set $Y_φ=φ(V)+U$, and define $P_φ(y)=\mathbb{E}[V\mid Y_φ=y]$ and $F_φ(x)=\mathbb{E}[P_φ(x+U)]$. We prove that, if for every $v\in\mathbb{R}$, the quantity $φ(v)$ maximises $x(v-F_φ(x))$ over $x\in\mathbb{R}$, then $φ$ is the identity function. This is the normalised one-period Kyle (1985) model of insider trading. It follows that Kyle's closed-form affine strategy is the unique equilibrium of the model for arbitrary Gaussian location and scale, and that its canonical competitive pricing rule is necessarily linear. This settles a long-standing question in financial economics. Boulatov, Kyle and Livdan (2005, 2013) introduced complex-analytic techniques to the problem. McLennan, Monteiro and Tourky (2017) proved a linear growth bound for $P_φ$, real-entire regularity of $F_φ$, and uniqueness when an equilibrium strategy agrees locally with a uniquely continuable analytic function. The present proof requires no regularity assumption on $φ$ beyond Borel measurability. Its argument is real-variable and probabilistic: the maximisation forces sharp upper and lower bounds for Gaussian-randomised monotone functions to coincide, and the corresponding equality cases admit only the identity function.

input: This research examines how reward models (RMs) trained through discriminative methods memorize information, using counterfactual memorization analysis across two human preference datasets. The findings reveal three core shortcomings in RMs: 1) memorization is disproportionately focused on clear-cut preference pairs with wide margins, 2) dataset-specific patterns are retained (such as particular model traits and user selection approaches), and 3) overly simplistic heuristic associations with human preference (such as response length and rule compliance) are applied when the models encounter unfamiliar preference pairs. Taken together, these findings indicate that building RMs from human preference data via discriminative training yields biased models that lack the depth necessary to reliably assess response quality across varying preference contexts.
target: This paper studies what discriminatively trained reward models (RMs) memorize by measuring counterfactual memorization on two human preference datasets. We show that RMs 1) misallocate memorization to easy, high margin preference pairs, 2) memorize dataset-specific shortcuts (e.g., model identity, user sampling strategy), and 3) overgeneralize simple heuristic correlates of human preference (e.g., length, compliance) when confronted with unseen preference pairs. Overall, our findings indicate that discriminative training of RMs from human preference data results in biased RMs not yet capable of judging response quality in context-dependent scenarios.

input:
In the myth of Hermes and Argus Panoptes, a giant possessing countless eyes is overcome not by strength but by cleverness: Hermes took on the guise of a shepherd and, using trickery and distraction, shut the creature's eyes one after another. The tale captures a lasting lesson—when facing an adversary of superior power, strategy outweighs raw force.

That lesson has a modern parallel in the struggle to outwit stylometric systems and surveillance tools, the many-eyed giants of our era. Writers seeking to safeguard the privacy of their texts must adopt intentional countermeasures. *TraceTarnish* is one such framework, built to conceal authorship attribution. This paper assesses which of its four elements—Translation, Obfuscation, Imitation, and Injection—is most effective at disrupting stylometric analysis. The findings clearly favor Injection: inserting zero-width Unicode characters, homoglyphs, and deliberate misspellings emerges as the most effective method for defeating stylometric detection and maintaining authorial anonymity.
target: What did it take for Hermes, the devout messenger of the Olympian gods, to slay Argus Panoptes, the multi-eyed giant of Greek myth? As the perfect guardian, Panoptes' legion of ever-watchful eyes proved difficult -- but not impossible -- to defeat. The centerpiece of Hermes' strategy was obfuscation and sabotage. Posing as a shepherd, Hermes sealed each of Panoptes' eyes -- eyes that would otherwise have alerted the fearsome giant to Hermes' plot -- and vanquished him. The moral of the story: when a challenger must surmount a formidable foe -- one far greater in stature and vastly more equipped -- crafty maneuvers are not merely advisable but indispensable for victory. In this work, the "challenger" is a collective leveraging adversarial tactics to overcome the "multi-eyed giant" of stylometric systems and surveillance apparatuses. To successfully claw back the privacy siphoned by the multi-eyed giant, the challenger must carefully evaluate their plan of attack, $\textit{TraceTarnish}$, and determine what does and does not work to anonymize the authorship of text. To that end, we conduct an ablation study of $\textit{TraceTarnish}$ to better understand which module -- Translation, Obfuscation, Imitation, or Injection -- best confounds a stylometric system. Our results indicate that the most effective approach was Injection, meaning that inserting zero-width Unicode characters, homoglyphs, and intentional misspellings neutralizes the indefatigable eyes long enough to claim the head of the all-seeing giant.

input: The Deep Galerkin Method (DGM) and Physics Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) are increasingly popular approaches within scientific machine learning for addressing partial differential equations (PDEs). Both techniques work by training a neural network to find the PDE solution, employing (stochastic) gradient descent to reduce the PDE residual produced by the network. However, since the PDE residual objective function is non-convex, a trained neural network could theoretically settle at a local minimum rather than a global one, meaning it might not actually solve the PDE. This raises important questions about the theoretical soundness of these methods, making it crucial to demonstrate that the trained network will actually approach the true PDE solution. For a specific category of semi-linear PDEs (where the nonlinearity involves the solution and its first-order derivatives), we demonstrate that neural networks optimized via gradient descent on the PDE residual objective will indeed converge toward the PDE solution.
target: The Deep Galerkin Method (DGM) and Physics Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) have become widely-used methods for solving partial differential equations (PDEs) in the rapidly growing field of scientific machine learning. In these methods, a neural network is trained to approximate the PDE solution by using (stochastic) gradient descent to minimize the PDE residual of the neural network. Due to the non-convexity of the PDE residual objective function, the trained neural network may, in principle, only converge to a local minimizer of the objective function (which would not be a solution of the PDE). Therefore, there is a longstanding question regarding the mathematical foundations of these algorithms, and it is highly valuable to establish that the trained neural network will converge to the PDE solution. For a class of semi-linear PDEs (nonlinear in the solution and its first derivative), we prove that neural networks trained with gradient descent to minimize the PDE residual objective function will converge to the PDE solution.

input: We investigate polynomial acceleration of the proximal point method (PPM) applied to maximal monotone inclusions, focusing on Anderson acceleration (AA) as a representative adaptive approach. We provide precise answers to three central questions. (i) For adaptive methods, the minimax complexity is exactly $d_0/(K+1)$ per $K$ resolvent evaluations. The averaged-reflection estimator achieves this upper bound; a matching lower bound comes from an explicit skew-adjoint operator whose resolvent has eigenvalues at the $(K+1)$-th roots of $-1$ and $\csc^2$-distributed masses, which forces every degree-$K$ polynomial method to satisfy $\|r(y_K)\|\ge 1/(K+1)$. The Fejér kernel is the unique optimal polynomial, and this construction also establishes a per-step lower limit. (ii) A sharp phase transition characterizes the behavior: Jackson-kernel polynomials deliver $O(d_0/(K^2 s))$ convergence when the spectral floor $s$ satisfies $sK\to\infty$, but at the critical threshold $s\asymp 1/K$ the fundamental limit reverts to $1/(K+1)$. These results generalize to normal operators and nonlinear operators of the form $M=S+N_C$. (iii) For linear problems, AA-PPM requires no safeguards; for nonlinear problems, verifying the $O(1/k)$ convergence rate requires exactly two oracle calls per iteration, and this number is minimal. Additionally, we refine and extend the theory for structured settings—including affine, strongly monotone, piecewise-affine, and Hölderian growth operators—and validate all theoretical predictions experimentally.
target: \noindent We study residual-polynomial acceleration of the proximal point method (PPM) for maximal monotone inclusions, with Anderson acceleration (AA) as the prototypical adaptive scheme. We answer three questions exactly. (i)~The minimax complexity over all adaptive methods is precisely $d_0/(K+1)$ per $K$ resolvent evaluations. The upper bound is attained by the averaged-reflection estimator; the matching lower bound uses an explicit skew-adjoint instance with resolvent eigenvalues at the roots of $u^{K+1}=-1$ and $\csc^2$-distributed masses, on which every degree-$K$ polynomial method satisfies $\|r(y_K)\|\ge 1/(K+1)$. The optimal polynomial is uniquely the Fejér kernel, and the same instance certifies a per-step floor. (ii)~A sharp phase transition separates regimes: Jackson-kernel polynomials achieve $O(d_0/(K^2 s))$ when the spectral floor $s$ satisfies $sK\to\infty$, while at the critical scale $s\asymp 1/K$ the barrier is exactly $1/(K+1)$. The picture extends to normal operators and the nonlinear family $M=S+N_C$. (iii)~On linear problems AA-PPM needs no safeguarding; on nonlinear problems certification of the $O(1/k)$ envelope requires exactly two oracle evaluations per iteration, and this factor is optimal. We also correct and complete the theory for structured problems---affine, strongly monotone, piecewise-affine, and Hölderian growth---and confirm all predictions numerically.

input: We study a three-dimensional model of charged-particle motion expressed using nonrelativistic momentum and construct a curve-reference exponential integrator (CREI) for it. The linear part of the system has a zero eigenvalue that is not semisimple, which prevents the system from being transformed into a form that meets the spectral conditions required by the standard locally linearized extended exponential integrator (LLEEI). To overcome this, we split the principal magnetic matrix into its kernel and range components and then apply an additional linear change of variables. Together, these steps recast the system into an equivalent form that contains a semisimple zero block alongside a constant skew-symmetric block with oscillatory behavior. Instead of expanding the nonlinear term around a single fixed point, the CREI expands it along the exact oscillatory solution curve. The variant CREI(k + 1) is obtained by retaining all monomials up to degree k in the expansion of the nonlinear term. We derive uniform error bounds for both local and global behavior and present reproducible numerical results that demonstrate convergence in the step size h and uniformity in the parameter ε.
target: We study a three-dimensional charged-particle dynamics model in the nonrelativistic momentum formulation and construct a curve-reference exponential integrator (CREI) for this system. Since the zero eigenvalue of linear section is not semisimple, the system after usual change of variables does not meet the spectral condition used in the classical locally linearized extended exponential integrator (LLEEI). A kernel-range decomposition of the dominant magnetic matrix and a further linear transformation reduce the equation to a system with a semisimple zero block and one constant skew-symmetric oscillatory block. The CREI expands the nonlinear term along the exact oscillatory curve rather than at a fixed point. Retaining monomials through degree k defines CREI(k + 1). We prove uniform local and global error bounds and present reproducible numerical experiments for convergence in h and uniformity in ε.

input:
This paper introduces a derivative-based finite volume Hermite WENO (HWENO) scheme for hyperbolic conservation laws. The method advances both the solution and its first-order derivatives in time together, using both quantities in the spatial reconstruction. A key difficulty in solving hyperbolic conservation laws is that discontinuities can appear in the computed solutions. At such discontinuities, derivatives may grow without bound, which can destabilize HWENO schemes. The original HWENO approach employed distinct stencil arrangements to reconstruct the primary equation and the derivative equation separately, seeking to restrict the effect of derivatives while preserving high-order accuracy. This approach, however, substantially raises computational cost and implementation complexity.

To address these drawbacks, the proposed method excludes derivative information from the target cell during spatial reconstruction, instead using the same reconstructed polynomial within the time-stepping process to control derivatives. This modification improves robustness compared to conventional HWENO schemes and permits a single unified stencil to be used throughout the derivative-based HWENO framework. The scheme additionally accommodates arbitrary positive linear weights that sum to one and retains a compact stencil width. Numerical experiments confirm that the proposed HWENO scheme achieves high-order accuracy, computational efficiency, sharp resolution, and robust performance.
target: In this paper, we propose a derivative-based finite volume Hermite WENO (HWENO) scheme for hyperbolic conservation laws, where both the solution and its first-order derivatives are evolved in time and utilized in spatial reconstructions. The key challenge for solving hyperbolic conservation laws is the possible emergence of discontinuities in the numerical solutions. When facing discontinuities, the derivatives can become excessively large, which may compromise the robustness of HWENO schemes. In the first HWENO scheme, different sets of stencils were adopted for reconstructing the governing equation and the derivative equation, respectively, aiming to reduce the influence of the derivatives while preserving high-order accuracy. However, this approach not only substantially increases computational cost but also introduces considerable algorithmic complexity. To overcome these limitations, we exclude the information of the target cell's derivatives from spatial reconstructions, while employing the same reconstructed polynomial during temporal evolution to limit the derivatives. This strategy enhances the robustness of traditional HWENO schemes and allows unified stencils within the derivative-based HWENO framework. Furthermore, the proposed scheme supports arbitrary positive linear weights that sum to one and maintains a compact stencil. Numerical results demonstrate the high-order accuracy, efficiency, high resolution, and robustness of the proposed HWENO scheme.

input: We introduce a Morse-theoretic method for constructing the Yang–Mills measure on the connection space of a compact Riemannian surface. This yields a direct, continuous formulation of the measure that had previously been derived via lattice approximations—by Chevyrev for flat tori, and by one of the authors with Nohra for general compact Riemannian surfaces. Our approach depends on introducing a Morse gauge and solving random cohomological equations tied to Morse–Smale vector fields. In doing so, we strengthen exponential convergence-to-equilibrium results for Morse–Smale gradient flows—originally established by two of the authors in connection with Ruelle spectra, and by Jia, Stewart, and Sverak in their work on simplified fluid mechanics models. By merging these random solutions with structural data from the Morse complex, we build a free Yang–Mills measure on the connection space. Standard stochastic differential equation methods enable us to rigorously define holonomies for random connections along a broad class of curves. We then suitably condition this free measure using the random holonomies to arrive at the Yang–Mills measure, compute its partition function, and identify the distribution of random holonomies under this measure, thereby recovering the classical results of Migdal, Witten, and Lévy.
target: We introduce a Morse theoretical approach to the construction of the Yang--Mills measure on the space of connections of a compact Riemannian surface. This provides a direct continuous version of this measure which was previously obtained through lattice approximations by Chevyrev in the case of the flat torus and by one of the authors and Nohra for general compact Riemannian surfaces. The starting point is the new notion of a Morse gauge together with the resolution of random cohomological equations associated to Morse--Smale vector fields. This is achieved by improving exponential convergence to equilibrium results for Morse--Smale gradient flows that were obtained by two of the authors in the context of the study of Ruelle spectra and by Jia, Stewart and Sverak in the context of simplified models from fluid mechanics. Combining these random solutions with the data given by the Morse complex, we introduce a free Yang-Mills measure on space of connections and, using classical tools from stochastic differential equations, we show how to make sense of holonomies for random connections along a large class of curves. Finally, by setting a proper conditioning of this free measure through these random holonomies, we define the Yang--Mills measure and we compute its partition function together with the law of random holonomies with respect to this measure, recovering the formulas from the works of Migdal, Witten and Lévy.

input:
This paper classifies all continuous solutions to the complex Kac--Bernstein functional equation
\[ f_1 ( u + v ) f_2 ( u - v ) f_1 ( u' + v' ) f_2 ( u' - v' ) = f_1 ( u + v' ) f_2 ( u - v' ) f_1 ( u' + v ) f_2 ( u' - v ) \]
over both $ \mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathbb{R}$. Using this classification for $\mathbb{Z}$, we extend the Kac--Bernstein theorem of Baryshnikov--Eisenberg--Stadje on the one-dimensional torus $\mathbb{T}$ beyond probability Borel measures to complex Borel measures. We also provide a parallel generalization of the classical Kac--Bernstein theorem on $\mathbb{R}$, broadening its scope from probability Borel measures to complex Borel measures.
target: In this paper, the continuous solutions of the complex Kac--Bernstein functional equation \[ f_1 ( u + v ) f_2 ( u - v ) f_1 ( u' + v' ) f_2 ( u' - v' ) = f_1 ( u + v' ) f_2 ( u - v' ) f_1 ( u' + v ) f_2 ( u' - v ) \] are classified for $ \mathbb{ Z } $ and $ \mathbb{ R } $. By using this classification for $ \mathbb{ Z } $, we consider a generalization of the Kac--Bernstein theorem on the one-dimensional torus $ \mathbb{ T } $ by Baryshnikov--Eisenberg--Stadje from probability Borel measures to complex Borel measures. Similarly, the original Kac--Bernstein theorem on $ \mathbb{ R } $ is generalized from probability Borel measures to complex Borel measures.

Let $(X,Y)$ be independent standard real Gaussian random variables, and let $P\in\mathbb{C}[X,Y]$ satisfy $\mathbb{E}\!\left(P(X,Y)^m\right)=0$ for all $m\ge1$. By passing to complex coordinates $Z=\frac{X+iY}{\sqrt{2}}$ and $W=\frac{X-iY}{\sqrt{2}}$, we show that the monomials of $P$ have strictly one-sided support with respect to the weight function $\operatorname{wt}(Z^aW^b)=a-b$. That is, every monomial appearing in $P$ carries either strictly positive weight or strictly negative weight. It follows that for any $Q\in\mathbb{C}[X,Y]$, one has $\mathbb{E}\!\left(Q(X,Y)P(X,Y)^m\right)=0$ whenever $m>\deg Q$. This proves the two-variable Gaussian Moments Conjecture with the explicit bound $m\ge\deg Q+1$.

The key tool in the proof is a prime-isolation theorem for exposed faces of the Newton polygon of $P$. By employing a $p$-adic valuation argument at moment indices of the form $m=qp$, we isolate the contribution of a chosen face and decouple it from all remaining multinomial terms. A Frobenius reduction then forces the constant terms of all positive powers of the associated one-variable Laurent polynomial to vanish. The Duistermaat–van der Kallen theorem ensures that the face has weights of uniform sign, and a two-dimensional convex-geometric argument rules out supports containing weights of both signs. Combined with the known one-variable case and explicit counterexamples for $n\ge3$, this precisely characterizes the dimensions in which the Gaussian Moments Conjecture holds.
